category: Formal, legal, Latin, and archaic prepositions

entries.meaning: A hybrid of English as and Latin per that grew up in nineteenth-century shipping and invoicing correspondence and never got out of it. It is not ungrammatical — only redundant, and dated in a way that makes business prose sound like a telegram.
examples: Shipped as per your instructions of the 14th.
The invoice was prepared as per the terms of the purchase order.
He was twenty minutes late, as per usual.
As per the attached schedule, delivery begins in March.
The specimens were tested as per ASTM D638.
As per our conversation, I have enclosed the revised bid.
As per usual, the meeting ran forty minutes over and settled nothing.

senses.head: In accordance with; as specified in — the ordinary commercial use
body: Shipped as per your instructions of the 14th.

senses.head: In the frozen jocular phrase as per usual, "as always."
body: He was twenty minutes late, as per usual.
examples: Shipped as per your instructions of the 14th.

entries.русский: согласно, в соответствии с — коммерч. канцеляризм, избыточный per; as per usual — «как всегда» (шутл.)
entries.register: business and commercial; widely condemned by usage guides
entries.complement: noun phrase — never a finite clause (✗ as per we agreed; write as per our agreement), never a gerund (✗ as per shipping it Tuesday; write as per the Tuesday shipping date). Before usual it takes no article: as per usual, and the phrase is frozen — you cannot extend the pattern (✗ as per normal, ✗ as per always).
entries.pattern: as per [noun phrase] · [clause], as per [noun phrase] · as per usual (fixed)
entries.contrast: As per adds nothing whatever to bare per, and every American usage guide from Fowler forward calls it commercialese. Prefer per, or better still plain according to or as you requested. The one form nobody objects to is the jocular fixed phrase as per usual, where the redundancy is the joke.
entries.variants: per is the plain replacement, and according to the plainer one; as per usual is the frozen jocular phrase; per usual is the American clipping of it
entries.see also: per, according to, in accordance with, pursuant to

entries.meaning: Opens the preamble of a multiparty contract — a credit agreement, a shareholders' agreement, a joint venture — which is where nearly every American transactional lawyer meets it, in the first line of the document rather than in running prose.
examples: THIS SHAREHOLDERS AGREEMENT is made by and among Corbin Holdings, Inc., the Investors listed on Schedule A, and the Founders.
The credit agreement was entered into by and among the Borrower, the Administrative Agent, and the Lenders party thereto.
This Amendment is made by and among the three original signatories and the successor trustee.
The escrow was established by and among buyer, seller, and the title company.
Settlement was reached by and among the class representatives, the defendant, and its two insurers.
When a fourth party joins the deal, the form book switches from by and between to by and among.
The operating agreement runs by and among the Company and each of its Members.
entries.русский: между (тремя и более сторонами) — юр., зачин преамбулы многостороннего договора
entries.register: legal — the preamble of a contract with three or more parties
entries.complement: two or more coordinated noun phrases naming the parties, and in practice three or more — never a finite clause (✗ by and among they signed yesterday), never a gerund (✗ by and among selling the plant). Each party is normally followed by its state of organization and a defined short name: a Delaware corporation ("Buyer").
entries.pattern: THIS AGREEMENT is made by and among [Party A], [Party B], and [Party C]. · entered into by and among [the parties]
entries.contrast: The choice between this and by and between is a headcount: American form books use between for two signatories and among for three or more. The schoolroom rule behind the convention is only half true — between is correct for any number when the relations are pairwise — but the drafting habit is real, and a reviewer will change between to among on a four-party signature block without asking. Both are doublets in which by alone would carry the load, and plain-language guides cut them to among. Distinguish by and through, which names an agent rather than the parties themselves.
entries.variants: among alone is the plain replacement; by and between is the two-party form; by, between and among and made and entered into by and among are the fuller form-book versions
entries.see also: by and between, by and through, between, amongst, by

entries.meaning: The first line of the body of nearly every American lease, purchase agreement, employment contract, and settlement agreement — and the phrase most often held up as the specimen of legal doubling that could simply be deleted.
examples: THIS LEASE is made by and between Palmetto Properties, LLC, and Devon Ruiz.
The agreement is by and between the City and the contractor named on the signature page.
Made and entered into this 4th day of June, by and between the Seller and the Buyer.
The collective bargaining agreement by and between the district and the teachers' union runs three years.
Older deeds read "made by and between the party of the first part and the party of the second part."
Drafting manuals tell you to delete by and and leave the between standing.
entries.русский: между (двумя сторонами) — юр., зачин преамбулы двустороннего договора
entries.register: legal — the preamble of a two-party contract
entries.complement: exactly two coordinated noun phrases joined by and — two parties, or two sides each made up of several persons. Never a finite clause (✗ by and between the parties agree as follows), never a gerund (✗ by and between leasing the premises).
entries.pattern: THIS LEASE is made by and between [Landlord] and [Tenant]. · an agreement by and between [Party A] and [Party B]
entries.contrast: Identical in force to plain between: the by adds nothing at all, and every plain-language drafting manual in America strikes it. Use by and among when three or more parties sign. Do not read by as naming the party who prepared the document — the phrase says nothing whatever about who drafted it, which matters because contra proferentem construes ambiguities against the drafter and the preamble will not tell you who that was. Distinguish by and through, the pleading formula that names counsel rather than the parties.
entries.variants: between alone is the plain replacement; made and entered into by and between is the fuller form; by and among is the multiparty version
entries.see also: by and among, by and through, between, by, under and pursuant to

entries.meaning: The standard American pleading formula that introduces the lawyer, guardian, or fiduciary through whom a party appears in court. Open almost any civil complaint filed in the United States and it is in the first line of the body.
examples: Plaintiff, by and through her attorneys, Ramirez & Hale LLP, alleges as follows.
The minor child appears by and through his guardian ad litem.
The estate acts by and through its personal representative.
Defendant, by and through undersigned counsel, moves to dismiss the amended complaint.
The tribe sued by and through its tribal council.
Notice was served by and through the registered agent of record.
entries.русский: в лице, через — юр. формула, называет представителя: адвоката, опекуна
entries.register: legal — pleadings and court filings
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a representative (counsel, guardian, trustee, agent) — never a clause, never a gerund. Always set off by commas inside the party designation.
entries.pattern: [party], by and through [attorney, guardian, or agent], [verb].
entries.contrast: A doublet in which by alone would carry the whole meaning; it survives because it sits in every pleading form book. It points the opposite way from on behalf of: by and through names the agent who does the acting, on behalf of names the principal the acting is done for. The related by his attorney is the older and shorter form still used in some state courts.
entries.variants: by and through her undersigned counsel is the fullest form; by alone is the plain-language replacement
entries.see also: on behalf of, by, under and pursuant to, vice

entries.meaning: Attributes a command to the office that issued it, and does so in a form short enough to fit on a placard. Americans meet it far more often on signs and posted notices than in running prose.
examples: NO TRESPASSING — By order of the Chief of Police.
The building was closed by order of the county health department.
By order of the court, all filings in this matter are sealed.
Flags will fly at half-staff through Sunday by order of the governor.
The road remains restricted by order of the Forest Service.
Occupancy is limited to 240 persons by order of the fire marshal.
entries.pronunciation note: fully reduced /baɪ ˈɔrɾɚ ə/ before a consonant · by-OR-der-uv
entries.русский: по приказу, по распоряжению — называет издавшую приказ инстанцию
entries.register: official and legal — signage, notices, court orders
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming an authority, normally a title rather than a bare personal name — never a clause, never a gerund (✗ by order of closing the road).
entries.pattern: By order of [authority]. (standing alone as a sign or notice) · [clause] by order of [authority].
entries.contrast: By order of names the issuing authority; pursuant to names the instrument. A parking sign reads By order of the Chief of Police; a brief reads pursuant to Municipal Code § 12-4. Its military cousin by direction of signs correspondence for a commander, and at the direction of is the softer civilian form that reports an instruction without invoking legal force.
entries.variants: by direction of (military correspondence); by authority of (older signage)
entries.see also: pursuant to, under and pursuant to, by virtue of, by

entries.meaning: Marks a proceeding brought by one side without the other present, or a communication with a judge behind an opponent's back — the second being the thing lawyers are ethically forbidden to do. Americans meet it in the great habeas cases Ex parte Milligan and Ex parte Young, in temporary-restraining-order practice, and in every judicial code of conduct.
examples: The court granted an ex parte temporary restraining order that afternoon.
Counsel is prohibited from any ex parte communication with the presiding judge.
Ex parte Quirin remains the leading military-commission case.
She applied ex parte for emergency custody of the children.
The order was vacated because it had been obtained ex parte.
Patent examiners handle ex parte reexamination without the challenger present.
Ex parte Milligan held that civilians could not be tried by military commission while the civil courts were open.
The judge disclosed the ex parte phone call on the record the next morning.

senses.head: In a case title: on the application of the party named, with no opponent before the court
body: Ex parte Quirin remains the leading military-commission case.

senses.head: Of a proceeding or an order: heard and decided on one side only
body: She applied ex parte for emergency custody.

senses.head: Of a communication: made to the judge behind the other side's back — the ethically forbidden sense
body: Counsel is prohibited from any ex parte contact with the court.
examples: The court granted an ex parte temporary restraining order that afternoon.
Counsel is prohibited from any ex parte communication with the presiding judge.
Ex parte Quirin remains the leading military-commission case.
She applied ex parte for emergency custody of the children.
The order was vacated because it had been obtained ex parte.
Patent examiners handle ex parte reexamination without the challenger present.
Ex parte Milligan held that civilians could not be tried by military commission while the civil courts were open.
The judge disclosed the ex parte phone call on the record the next morning.

entries.русский: юр. в одностороннем порядке — по заявлению одной стороны, без участия другой
entries.register: legal
entries.complement: as a preposition, only a party's name, and only in a case title (Ex parte Milligan). Everywhere else in American practice it is an adjective (an ex parte motion) or an adverb (the judge ruled ex parte) and takes no object at all. Never a clause, never a gerund.
entries.pattern: Ex parte [name of the applying party] (case title) · an ex parte [motion / order / communication] (attributive) · [verb] ex parte (adverbial)
entries.contrast: Latin ex parte is "from a party" — one side only. Its opposite is inter partes, both sides participating, which belongs to the frozen family under inter. Do not confuse it with ex post facto (retroactive, and constitutionally forbidden for criminal statutes) or with the commercial ex of ex works.
entries.variants: Ex p. in older reporters; ex parte is set in italics in most American style manuals but roman in the Bluebook when part of a case name
entries.see also: inter, ex, pro, in re

entries.respell: the full Latin ex relatione is /ɛks ˌrɛləʃiˈoʊni/
entries.meaning: Names the person who set a lawsuit going in somebody else's name. An American meets it in the caption of a whistleblower case, in state mandamus practice where a citizen sues in the name of the state, and in habeas reports from before the 1960s.
examples: United States ex rel. Schutte v. SuperValu Inc. turned on what the defendants actually believed.
The caption reads State ex rel. Vasquez v. Board of Elections.
Habeas petitions were once styled United States ex rel. Jones v. Warden of Sing Sing.
The relator's name stays in the caption after ex rel. even once the government intervenes.
Ohio's mandamus docket is full of ex rel. captions, because the citizen sues in the name of the state.
Lawyers say "ex rel" out loud; nobody says ex relatione.
American style writes it ex rel. with a period and sets it roman inside a case name.
entries.pronunciation note: eks-REL · no weak form: quoted Latin keeps its full vowels
entries.русский: юр. по заявлению, от имени (лат. ex relatione) — иск подан от имени государства
entries.register: legal — case names and citation
entries.complement: the name of the relator — the private person or public officer on whose information the action is brought — standing between the nominal plaintiff and the v. Never a clause, never a gerund, and it does not govern an ordinary noun phrase in running prose (✗ the suit was brought ex rel. a whistleblower; write on the relation of a whistleblower).
entries.pattern: [sovereign or nominal plaintiff] ex rel. [relator] v. [defendant] · reported ex rel. [relator]
entries.contrast: Latin ex relatione, "on the relation of" — that is, on the information of someone who is not the nominal plaintiff. It is the caption of the American qui tam action: under the False Claims Act the United States is the plaintiff and the whistleblower is the relator, so the case reads United States ex rel. Schutte v. SuperValu. Keep it clear of its shelfmates: ex parte says only one side was heard, sub nom. (see sub) says the case was reported under a different name on the way up, and in re says there was no adversary at all. Americans read it aloud as "ex rel," never expanded.
entries.variants: ex relatione is the full Latin and is effectively never written out; on the relation of is the English; qui tam names the kind of action rather than the caption; older habeas petitions used the same form (United States ex rel. Jones v. Warden)
entries.see also: ex parte, ex, sub, in re, versus

entries.meaning: A fossil of the Old English habit of putting the object first and letting an adverb swallow it. It is the reason contract prose can refer to itself without ever naming itself, and the reason non-lawyers find contracts unreadable.
examples: The Seller's obligations hereunder survive termination of this Agreement.
Any notice given hereunder must be in writing and sent by certified mail.
Payments due hereunder bear interest at six percent from the due date.
Nothing hereunder creates a partnership or joint venture between the parties.
The Licensee's rights hereunder are personal and non-transferable.
Each party shall bear its own costs incurred hereunder.
entries.русский: юр. по настоящему договору — «по этому документу»; дополнения не берёт
entries.register: legal — contract drafting
entries.complement: none. This word takes no object. Its object is already inside it: here means "this document," so hereunder is a complete phrase meaning "under this agreement." Writing hereunder this contract is an error, and so is hereunder to Section 4.
entries.pattern: [noun phrase] hereunder · [verb phrase] hereunder · rights and obligations hereunder
entries.contrast: Hereunder points at the document you are reading; thereunder points at some other instrument just named. Mixing them up changes what a contract means. The whole family is a preposition welded to a pointing word — hereof, hereto, herein, hereby, hereinafter, hereunder, herewith, hereinabove — and every plain-language drafting manual in America tells you to replace each of them with under this Agreement, to this Agreement, and so on.
entries.variants: under this Agreement is the plain-language replacement; the here- family, every member of which takes no object of its own: hereof, hereto, herein, hereby, herewith, hereinafter, hereinbefore, hereinabove, heretofore
entries.see also: thereunder, in witness whereof, under and pursuant to, under

entries.meaning: The phrase that opens the operative clause of nearly every American contract and deed, and the hinge on which the enforceability of the whole document turns.
examples: In consideration of the sum of ten dollars and other good and valuable consideration, Grantor conveys the following described tract.
The release was signed in consideration of a lump-sum severance payment.
In consideration of the mutual covenants set forth herein, the parties agree as follows.
She accepted the easement in consideration of a one-time payment of $4,000.
The sentence was reduced in consideration of his cooperation with the government.
In consideration of her thirty years of service, the board voted her a full pension.
The policy was rewritten in consideration of the flood risk along the coast.
In consideration of releasing all claims against the estate, she received a lump sum of $250,000.

senses.head: Contract law: in exchange for; as the bargained-for price of a promise
body: In consideration of the sum of ten dollars, Grantor conveys the following tract.

senses.head: General formal prose: in view of; taking account of
body: The sentence was reduced in consideration of his cooperation.
examples: In consideration of the sum of ten dollars and other good and valuable consideration, Grantor conveys the following described tract.
The release was signed in consideration of a lump-sum severance payment.

entries.русский: юр. в обмен на, за встречное предоставление; книжн. ввиду, принимая во внимание
entries.register: legal in the contract sense; formal general prose in the other
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund — never a finite clause (✗ in consideration of he paid the deposit). For a clause you must write in consideration of the fact that, and you should usually write because instead. A verb after of takes the -ing form and nothing else: in consideration of releasing all claims, never ✗ in consideration of to release all claims.
entries.pattern: In consideration of [noun phrase], [clause]. · [clause] in consideration of [noun phrase] · in consideration of [verb-ing]
entries.contrast: Two different words wear the same coat. In contract law consideration is the technical name for the bargained-for exchange, and this phrase introduces it — a promise without consideration is unenforceable, so the words are doing legal work, not decorating. In ordinary formal prose it means "in view of, out of regard for," close to in light of. Keep it clear of out of consideration for, which means "out of politeness toward" and is a different idiom entirely.
entries.variants: for and in consideration of (the fuller conveyancing doublet); in consideration whereof (older)
entries.see also: in exchange for, in light of, in view of, for, subject to

entries.meaning: Sets out what happens when the first arrangement fails. It is the hinge of a will, of a power of appointment, and of every clause that has to name a fallback.
examples: In default of issue, the remainder passes to the testator's nieces and nephews.
The trust names takers in default of appointment, which is what saves the gift if the power is never exercised.
In default of payment within thirty days, the entire balance becomes immediately due.
In default of an appearance by the defendant, the clerk may enter judgment.
In default of agreement between the two appraisers, a third is named by the court.
In default of a written contract, the parties are left with whatever the emails prove.
The policy lapses in default of the annual premium.
In default of nomination by the union, the arbitrator is drawn from the standing panel.

senses.head: Wills and trusts: if the named person or class fails
body: In default of issue, the property passes to my brother's children.

senses.head: Contracts: if the required act is not done in time
body: In default of payment within thirty days, the whole balance falls due.

senses.head: Procedure: if nobody appears, or nobody agrees
body: In default of agreement, the matter goes to arbitration.

entries.pronunciation note: fully reduced /ɪn dəˈfɔlt ə/ before a consonant · in-dih-FAWLT-uv
entries.русский: юр. за неимением, при отсутствии — если названное лицо или действие отсутствует
entries.register: formal and legal — wills, trusts, contracts, and court rules
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund — never a finite clause (✗ in default of he pays the premium; write in default of payment). The of is a preposition, so a verb after it must be an -ing form: in default of paying the premium, never ✗ in default of to pay the premium. The object names the act or event that fails to happen, not the person who fails: in default of issue, in default of appointment, in default of agreement.
entries.pattern: In default of [noun phrase], [clause]. · [clause] in default of [noun phrase] · in default of [verb-ing]
entries.contrast: It means "if that does not happen," not "because somebody defaulted." The bare adverbial in default, with no of, is the other word — a defendant who never answers is in default — and default on takes the loan or obligation as its object. Its plain neighbors are in the absence of, which is neutral about whose fault the gap is, and failing, which is the one-word equivalent and much the shorter. Estate drafters use one collocation above all others: in default of issue, meaning "if he leaves no children."
entries.variants: failing is the one-word equivalent; in the absence of and for want of are the plainer phrases; in default whereof is the older self-pointing form; in default of appointment and in default of issue are the fixed drafting collocations
entries.see also: failing, in the absence of, subject to, save and except, without prejudice to

entries.meaning: The testimonium clause — the fixed line that opens the signature block of an American contract, deed, affidavit, or gubernatorial proclamation. It is not a productive preposition at all: it is a fossil you will read a thousand times and never build a new sentence with.
examples: In witness whereof, the parties have executed this Agreement as of the date first written above.
In witness whereof, I have hereunto set my hand and caused the Great Seal of the State of Ohio to be affixed.
In witness whereof, the undersigned has caused this Deed to be executed by its duly authorized officer.
The notary's certificate appeared immediately below the in witness whereof line.
In witness whereof, the Corporation has caused these presents to be signed this 3rd day of April.
Older forms open the clause in testimony whereof rather than in witness whereof.
entries.русский: юр. в удостоверение чего — застывшая формула перед подписями в договоре
entries.register: legal — execution and testimonium clauses
entries.complement: none. Whereof already contains its object — it means "of which," pointing back at the document — so the phrase is complete as it stands. It is always followed by a comma and then a full clause, never by a noun phrase (✗ in witness whereof this deed).
entries.pattern: In witness whereof, [the parties have executed this Agreement as of the date first written above].
entries.contrast: The where- family is the third leg of a three-part system: hereunder points at the document you are holding, thereunder at another one just named, and whereof at the thing last mentioned. Its relatives are whereby, wherein, whereas, whereupon, wherefore, whereto. The variant in witness thereof is usually a drafting slip rather than a genuine alternative — thereof points away from the document that is being signed, which is not what the signer means.
entries.variants: in testimony whereof (state seals and notarial certificates); witness my hand and seal (the shorter American form); the where- family, which likewise governs nothing: whereof, whereby, wherein, whereas, whereupon, wherefore, whereto
entries.see also: hereunder, thereunder, in consideration of, of

entries.meaning: The reservation formula of American deed drafting, and above all of Texas and Oklahoma oil-and-gas conveyances, where a grantor uses it to keep the minerals while selling the surface. Read one mineral deed and you will meet it in the first paragraph.
examples: Grantor conveys the surface estate, save and except all oil, gas, and other minerals in and under said land.
The lease covers the entire section, save and except forty acres surrounding the homestead.
All fixtures pass with the sale, save and except the walk-in cooler and the display cases.
Save and except the easement described in Exhibit B, the tract is unencumbered.
The assignment transfers every well on the lease, save and except the Jones No. 2.
Grantor conveys all of Lot 7, save and except that portion previously dedicated to the county for road purposes.
entries.русский: юр. за исключением — дублет в актах о передаче недвижимости, = except
entries.register: legal — deeds, conveyances, oil-and-gas instruments
entries.complement: noun phrase — never a clause, never a gerund. The object is the thing carved out of the grant, and it must be described with the same precision as the grant itself.
entries.pattern: [granting clause], save and except [noun phrase] · Save and except [noun phrase], [clause].
entries.contrast: A doublet in which both halves mean the same thing: save is the native-English member and except the Latin-derived one, paired by the medieval habit of doubling a word with its Romance twin (will and testament, free and clear, give, devise and bequeath). Ordinary writing wants except alone — and note the division of labor between except and except for: bare except subtracts from a word already in the sentence (everyone except Marcia signed), while except for stands outside the whole clause and qualifies it (Except for the roof, the house is sound). Note also that bare save has a second life as a conjunction taking a clause (save that he arrived late); the doublet does not — save and except is a preposition and nothing else. Finally, a save and except clause reserves an interest to the grantor, while an exception to a warranty merely limits what is being warranted — Texas courts have decided a great many cases on that difference.
entries.variants: saving and excepting (the participial form); less and except (equally common in mineral deeds); reserving unto Grantor (the reservation, as opposed to exception, wording)
entries.see also: save, except, excepting, with the exception of, subject to

entries.meaning: The most productive word in this file and the only one an ordinary American uses without noticing. Three senses run through it, and they shade into one another: a condition, an authority, and an exposure.
examples: The offer is subject to a satisfactory home inspection.
Subject to shareholder approval, the merger closes in April.
All fares and schedules are subject to change without notice.
Federal contractors are subject to the same disclosure rules as agencies.
The territory remained subject to the crown for another century.
Any amount subject to withholding must be reported on Form 1099.
The coast is subject to flooding every spring.
He has been subject to migraines since childhood.
The permit is granted subject to the applicant posting a bond.
Closing is subject to obtaining a firm commitment from the lender by June 1.

senses.head: Conditional on; not final until something else happens
body: The offer is subject to a satisfactory inspection.

entries.русский: при условии, с учётом; подчинённый (власти, юрисдикции); подверженный чему-то
entries.register: formal and legal, but fully current in general American English
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund — never a finite clause (subject to the board approves it; write subject to the board's approval or subject to approval by the board). ✗ The to is a preposition here, not the infinitive marker, so a verb after it must be an -ing form: subject to obtaining a permit, never ✗ subject to obtain a permit — the same trap as look forward to seeing you, object to being questioned, and accustomed to working late. The gerund may carry its own subject in the possessive or objective case: subject to the applicant's posting a bond. Pronoun objects take the objective case: subject to them, never ✗ subject to they.
entries.pattern: Subject to [noun phrase], [clause]. · [clause] subject to [noun phrase] · [noun] subject to [noun phrase] · subject to [verb-ing]
entries.contrast: Stress separates the preposition from the verb it looks like: the preposition and adjective are SUB-ject /ˈsʌbdʒɪkt/, while the verb meaning "to expose someone to something" is sub-JECT /səbˈdʒɛkt/ (they subjected him to a search). Against its neighbors, subject to makes the main event conditional and revocable — the condition can still undo it later — where contingent on and dependent on merely make it conditional up front, and pursuant to makes it authorized. Subject to change and subject to availability are fixed phrases.
entries.variants: contingent on and dependent on are the near equivalents for the conditional sense; subject to change, subject to availability, and subject to approval are fixed phrases; subject thereto is the legal-fossil form that points back at a document already named
entries.see also: pursuant to, without prejudice to, in accordance with, to, save and except

entries.meaning: The pointing twin of hereunder, and the workhorse of American regulatory citation, where the standard formula is the Act and the regulations promulgated thereunder.
examples: The Act and the regulations promulgated thereunder apply to all interstate carriers.
The lease and the rights granted thereunder were assigned in 2019.
Any claim arising thereunder is barred by the statute of limitations.
The trust and the powers conferred thereunder terminate at her death.
He cited the treaty and two decisions rendered thereunder.
Section 10(b) and Rule 10b-5 promulgated thereunder prohibit securities fraud.
entries.русский: юр. на его основании, по нему — отсылает к другому, ранее названному документу
entries.register: legal and regulatory
entries.complement: none — the object is incorporated. There points at a statute, contract, or provision already named, so thereunder means "under that." Thereunder the statute is an error.
entries.pattern: [noun phrase] thereunder · [verb phrase] thereunder · the Act and the regulations promulgated thereunder
entries.contrast: Hereunder points at the document you are reading; thereunder points at some other instrument just mentioned. Drafters confuse the two constantly, and the mistake is substantive, not stylistic — it can redirect an entire obligation. The there- family runs thereof, thereto, therein, thereby, thereafter, thereunder, therewith, theretofore, thereupon.
entries.variants: under that Agreement / under the Act are the plain-language replacements; the there- family, all of them objectless: thereof, thereto, therein, thereby, therewith, thereafter, theretofore, thereupon
entries.see also: hereunder, in witness whereof, under and pursuant to, under

entries.meaning: Derives an action from a written authority, twice over. The only reason to know it is that you will read it, not write it.
examples: The sale is made under and pursuant to the terms of the settlement agreement.
Bonds issued under and pursuant to the Indenture rank equally with one another.
The trustee acts under and pursuant to Article VII of the trust instrument.
Notice was given under and pursuant to Section 1692g of the Act.
The property was sold under and pursuant to a decree of foreclosure entered March 4.
Under and pursuant to the authority vested in me by the Constitution, I hereby proclaim...
entries.русский: юр. на основании, в соответствии с — дублет, полностью = pursuant to
entries.register: legal
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming an instrument or a source of authority — a statute, an agreement, an order, a section number. Never a clause, never a gerund.
entries.pattern: [clause] under and pursuant to [statute / agreement / order] · Under and pursuant to [instrument], [clause].
entries.contrast: A pure doublet: pursuant to already means "under." It persists because form books carry it, and it is the first phrase struck by every plain-language style guide, including the federal courts' own. Distinguish by order of, which names the issuing authority rather than the instrument, and in accordance with, which claims conformity rather than derivation.
entries.variants: under alone is the plain-language replacement; pursuant to and in accordance with (a longer doublet of the same kind)
entries.see also: pursuant to, by order of, in accordance with, thereunder, hereunder

entries.meaning: Reserves a right instead of surrendering it. It is the drafter's way of saying that doing this now does not cost me that later, and it is why a party can pay under protest, or settle one claim while keeping another alive.
examples: Without prejudice to its right to appeal, the company paid the assessed penalty.
The case was dismissed without prejudice to refiling in state court.
Without prejudice to the foregoing, Buyer may terminate on ten days' written notice.
She accepted the interim payment without prejudice to her larger claim.
The stipulation is without prejudice to any party's position on the merits.
Counsel appeared without prejudice to the pending jurisdictional objection.
The parties settled the fee dispute without prejudice to litigating the merits in the pending action.

senses.head: Reserving a substantive right that the present act might otherwise waive
body: Without prejudice to its right to appeal, the company paid the penalty.

senses.head: In litigation: leaving a claim, a defense, or a position free to be raised again later
body: The case was dismissed without prejudice to refiling in state court.
examples: Without prejudice to its right to appeal, the company paid the assessed penalty.
The case was dismissed without prejudice to refiling in state court.

entries.русский: юр. без ущерба для — сохраняя право, которое иначе считалось бы утраченным
entries.register: legal
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund — never a finite clause (✗ without prejudice to she may appeal; write without prejudice to her right to appeal). The to is a preposition here too, so a verb after it takes -ing: without prejudice to refiling, never ✗ without prejudice to refile.
entries.pattern: Without prejudice to [noun phrase], [clause]. · [clause] without prejudice to [noun phrase] · dismissed without prejudice (adverbial, no object)
entries.contrast: The bare adverbial without prejudice, with no to, is far commoner and means something narrower: a case dismissed without prejudice can be refiled, one dismissed with prejudice cannot. British practice also uses without prejudice to mark settlement correspondence inadmissible; in an American court that label has no magic effect, and lawyers write for settlement purposes only under Rule 408. Compare the ordinary privative without, which merely subtracts.
entries.variants: without prejudice (adverbial, no object — the commoner form); without waiving (the same reservation in plainer words)
entries.see also: without, subject to, notwithstanding, irrespective of

entries.meaning: Latin "to, toward, for." Like inter and pro it never became a free English preposition and survives only welded to the noun it governs — but the phrases it is welded into are among the commonest Latin tags in American public life.
examples: The mayor named an ad hoc committee to study the flooding.
Scheduling is done ad hoc, which is why nobody knows when the truck comes.
The court appointed a guardian ad litem to represent the child's interests.
An administrator ad litem was named because the executor had a conflict.
County property taxes are levied ad valorem on the assessed value.
Congress replaced the specific duty with an ad valorem rate of six percent.
She served as chargé d'affaires ad interim for eight months.
The appointment was ad interim and lapsed when the Senate reconvened.
The complaint's ad damnum clause demanded ten million dollars.
Counsel repeated the point ad nauseam until the judge cut him off.

senses.head: Ad hoc: for this one purpose; improvised, not systematic
body: The mayor named an ad hoc committee on flooding.

senses.head: Ad litem: for the lawsuit — of a representative appointed for the case alone
body: The court appointed a guardian ad litem for the child.

senses.head: Ad valorem: according to value — the tax and customs sense
body: Property taxes are levied ad valorem.

senses.head: Ad interim: for the time being; in the interval
body: She served as chargé d'affaires ad interim.

senses.head: Frozen phrases of extent: ad damnum, ad nauseam, ad infinitum
body: The ad damnum clause demanded ten million dollars.

entries.русский: лат. «к, для» — живёт только в оборотах: ad hoc, ad litem, ad valorem, ad nauseam
entries.register: legal, academic, and commercial; a bound element, never a free preposition
entries.complement: only the Latin noun the phrase was borrowed with — ad hoc, ad litem, ad valorem, ad interim, ad damnum, ad idem, ad nauseam. It cannot govern an English noun phrase (✗ ad the committee; write to the committee), and it never takes a clause or a gerund.
entries.pattern: an ad hoc [committee / arrangement] · guardian ad litem · ad valorem [tax / duty] · [officer] ad interim · the ad damnum clause
entries.contrast: Latin ad is "to, toward, for the purpose of," and it is the ad- of adjacent, adhere, and administer; English to and for took the whole job, so the free preposition never entered the language. Against pro, the other Latin "for": pro is "on behalf of" — an attorney serves pro bono, for the public good — while ad is "for the purpose of," so a guardian ad litem is appointed for the lawsuit and nothing else. Watch the American stress and vowels: ad hoc is /æd ˈhɑk/ here, not the classical /ɑd ˈhoʊk/.
entries.variants: ad- as a productive English prefix (adjoin, adjunct, advert); ad hoc has become an ordinary English adjective and adverb and is no longer felt as Latin; ad valorem is the opposite of a specific duty
entries.see also: pro, de, sub, to, for

entries.meaning: Latin "at, among, in the works of." Only the bibliographic sense reached English, and it stayed in the disciplines that spend their days with texts surviving inside other texts.
examples: Heraclitus, fr. 12 Diels, apud Arius Didymus.
The saying survives only apud Clement of Alexandria.
Chrysippus, apud Plutarch, De Stoicorum repugnantiis 1035a.
The editor prints the fragment apud Stobaeus and marks the attribution doubtful.
Cited apud Migne, Patrologia Graeca 44, col. 1128.
American law reviews want quoted in; apud now lives in classical and theological journals.
Where a manuscript reading survives only in a commentary, the apparatus records it apud the commentator.
entries.pronunciation note: AP-uud · no weak form: it is quoted Latin and keeps its full vowels
entries.русский: лат. «у, в сочинении» — науч. цит. по, приводится по (автору, сохранившему текст)
entries.register: scholarly citation — classics, patristics, medieval history, and bibliography
entries.complement: the name of the author or work in whose text the quoted matter is preserved, or a full citation of it — never a clause, never a gerund. It cannot govern an ordinary English noun phrase in running prose (✗ apud the library): Latin's household sense went into French, not into English.
entries.pattern: [quoted author or fragment] apud [the author who preserves it] · quoted apud [work and page]
entries.contrast: Latin apud is "at the house of, in the presence of, in the writings of" — the Latin twin of chez, which kept the household sense while apud kept only the bibliographic one. In a footnote it does the work of as quoted in or as cited in, and it is used for an honest reason: you have seen not the original but the later author who quotes it. Keep it apart from sensu, which reports the meaning an author gave a name rather than the text that preserves a passage, and from cf., which asks the reader to compare rather than reporting where something is found.
entries.variants: ap. is the abbreviation used in a critical apparatus; as quoted in and as cited in are the English equivalents most American journals now require
entries.see also: sensu, cf., sub verbo, chez, supra

entries.meaning: Latin confer, "compare." Strictly it is an imperative verb, but on the page it behaves like a preposition: it stands immediately in front of a reference and governs it.
examples: Cf. Restatement (Second) of Torts § 402A (imposing strict liability on sellers of defective products).
See Gray, 118 F.3d at 1102; cf. Ellison, 924 F.2d at 878 (reaching the same result on other grounds).
The brief cites three cases in support and one, with a cf., by analogy only.
The specimen was logged as Tyrannosaurus cf. rex until the skull could be prepared.
A jaw labeled Equus aff. caballus is close to the modern horse and probably not the same species.
Chicago style sets cf. roman and lowercase inside a note.
A student who writes cf. where he means e.g. is promising an analogy he has not made.

senses.head: Citation signal: compare the authority cited, which supports the point by analogy rather than directly
body: Cf. Restatement (Second) of Torts § 402A.

senses.head: Taxonomy, between genus and species: this specimen resembles that species but cannot be identified with certainty
body: The bone was catalogued as Equus cf. caballus.

entries.pronunciation note: read aloud as the two letters, or as compare; the full Latin confer is /ˈkɑnfɜr/ and is never said
entries.русский: ср. (сравни) — отсылка к источнику, подтверждающему мысль косвенно, по аналогии
entries.register: scholarly and legal citation; taxonomic Latin
entries.type: marginal (a Latin imperative working as a citation signal)
entries.complement: a citation, a page or section reference, or — in a taxonomic name — the species epithet standing between genus and species. Never a finite clause (✗ cf. the court held otherwise; put that in a parenthetical), never a gerund. In American legal citation the Bluebook expects an explanatory parenthetical after it, because the reader cannot otherwise tell what the analogy is meant to be.
entries.pattern: Cf. [citation] ([parenthetical explaining the analogy]). · see [source]; cf. [source] · [Genus] cf. [species] (taxonomy)
entries.contrast: On the American citation scale it stands on the supporting side but at arm's length: see → see also → cf. → but see → contra. Cf. says the authority supports the point by analogy, not directly. In taxonomy the abbreviation concedes something else entirely — doubt about a specimen — and it is paired there with aff.: Genus cf. species means "compare: probably this species, though the material will not prove it," while Genus aff. species means "close to that species, and probably not it." The error to avoid everywhere is writing cf. for e.g. (for example) or i.e. (that is); the three are not interchangeable, and cf. alone asks the reader to do comparative work.
entries.variants: aff. (Latin affinis, "related to") is the taxonomic sibling; cp. is the older British abbreviation; confer is the full Latin and is never written out; sp. and indet. mark other degrees of taxonomic uncertainty
entries.see also: contra, supra, infra, apud, sensu

entries.meaning: French for "at the home or establishment of," borrowed whole and never naturalized. Americans meet it on restaurant awnings (Chez Panisse), in society columns, and in the mock-anthropological register of magazine profiles.
examples: We're eating chez Marie tonight.
Dinner is at eight, chez nous.
Things have been tense chez Wilson since the election.
He spent the whole summer chez his grandparents outside Lyon.
The recipe came from a cook I met chez Panisse.
Chez the Bernsteins, nobody went to bed before midnight.
Chez the Roosevelts, politics was simply the family business.

senses.head: At the home or place of business of
body: We're eating chez Marie tonight.

senses.head: In the world of; over at — of a household, a family, or an institution, and always a little arch
body: Things have been tense chez Wilson since the election.
examples: We're eating chez Marie tonight.
Dinner is at eight, chez nous.
Things have been tense chez Wilson since the election.

entries.русский: у (кого-то дома), в доме у — из французского, часто с оттенком шутливой манерности
entries.register: literary or jocular; mildly affected in plain American prose
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a person, a family, a household, or an establishment — a bare personal name (chez Marie), a family name with the article (chez the Bernsteins), a possessive-marked noun phrase (chez his grandparents), or a French pronoun in the fixed forms chez moi, chez nous, chez toi, chez lui, chez elle. Never an English pronoun (✗ chez me; say at my place), never a clause, never a gerund.
entries.pattern: chez [name] · chez [moi / nous / lui / elle] · chez [family or institution] (extended sense)
entries.contrast: English at plus a possessive does exactly the same work with no accent and no wink: at Marie's. What chez adds is tone. Note the extended jocular sense "in the world of, over at," where the object is a household, a family, or an institution — things are tense chez Wilson — which has no one-word English equivalent.
entries.variants: chez soi ("at one's own home," reflexive); chez-soi as a noun in French, not borrowed into English
entries.see also: à la, at, with

entries.meaning: A Latin "against" that survives in three narrow trades and nowhere else. Note that the free-standing form is not a preposition at all but an adverb, since the thing it opposes is already on the page.
examples: Contra Smith v. Jones, 410 F.3d 112, 118 (9th Cir. 2005).
Accumulated depreciation is a contra asset account.
The doctrine of contra proferentem construes an ambiguity against the party that drafted it.
Two judges of the panel wrote contra, and the majority did not answer them.
Every argument pro was met within the hour by one contra.
The brief cites four cases in support and, contra, none at all.
Allowance for doubtful accounts is a contra account netted against receivables.
Contra Restatement (Second) of Contracts § 90, which the panel never cited.

senses.head: Citation signal, governing a full citation: the authority cited flatly contradicts the proposition just stated
body: Contra Smith v. Jones, 410 F.3d 112.

senses.head: Accounting, attributive: offsetting; paired with another account and netted against it
body: Accumulated depreciation is a contra asset account.

senses.head: Free-standing adverb or noun, with no object at all: on the other side; against
body: Two judges of the panel wrote contra.
examples: Contra Smith v. Jones, 410 F.3d 112, 118 (9th Cir. 2005).

entries.русский: юр. «напротив» — источник прямо опровергает сказанное; бухг. контр-, встречный
entries.register: legal, academic, and accounting; never conversational
entries.complement: in the citation use, a full case or source citation rather than an ordinary noun phrase. In the free use it is an adverb or a noun with no object at all (two justices wrote contra; the pros and contras). Never a clause, never a gerund.
entries.pattern: Contra [citation]. (a signal introducing disagreeing authority) · a contra [account / entry] (attributive) · pro and contra (adverbial pair)
entries.contrast: Latin contra is the ancestor of English against and of counter-, and it lost to both. In American legal citation it is the strongest negative signal on a scale that runs see → cf. → but see → contra: contra means the cited authority flatly contradicts the proposition. In accounting, a contra account is one that offsets another, as accumulated depreciation offsets an asset. The Nicaraguan Contras took their name from Spanish contrarrevolucionario and have nothing to do with the preposition's ordinary use.
entries.variants: contra- as an English prefix (contraindicate, contraflow, contradistinction); contra proferentem (construed against the drafter)
entries.see also: against, pro, versus, ex parte

entries.meaning: Latin "in the presence of." Where an American meets it: a post-conviction petition, an old English report, and Horace's coram populo, "out in front of the people."
examples: He petitioned for a writ of error coram nobis to clear the conviction long after the sentence had run.
Korematsu's conviction was vacated on a coram nobis petition in 1983.
Because the sentence was fully served, habeas was unavailable and only coram nobis remained.
A judgment entered coram non judice is a nullity and may be attacked at any time.
Most states abolished coram vobis when they adopted a single post-conviction statute.
Horace's rule was that the horrors happen offstage, not coram populo.
The motion is captioned as a petition for a writ of error coram nobis under the All Writs Act.

senses.head: Coram nobis: before us — the writ that reopens a conviction on a fact the court never knew
body: He petitioned for a writ of error coram nobis thirty years later.

senses.head: Coram non judice: before one who is not a judge — of a judgment void for want of jurisdiction
body: A decree entered coram non judice binds nobody.

senses.head: Coram populo: in public; in front of the crowd — the literary use
body: Nothing shameful was to be done coram populo.
examples: He petitioned for a writ of error coram nobis to clear the conviction long after the sentence had run.

entries.pronunciation note: KOR-um · no weak form: quoted Latin keeps its full vowels
entries.русский: лат. «перед, в присутствии» — только в оборотах: coram nobis, coram populo
entries.register: legal, with one literary survival; a bound element, never a free preposition
entries.complement: only the Latin noun fixed to it — coram nobis, coram vobis, coram non judice, coram populo. It cannot govern an English noun phrase (✗ coram the judge; write before the judge), and it never takes a clause or a gerund.
entries.pattern: a writ of error coram nobis · a judgment coram non judice · coram populo
entries.contrast: Latin coram is "in the presence of, face to face with," and English before took the whole job. The American survival is the writ of error coram nobis — "before us," meaning the court's own record — which federal courts may still issue under the All Writs Act to correct a conviction after the sentence has been served; its twin coram vobis, "before you," went to the reviewing court, and most states have abolished the distinction. Coram non judice is not a place but a verdict: it says the tribunal had no jurisdiction, so its judgment is a nullity. Distinguish ex parte, which is about who was heard rather than who did the hearing.
entries.variants: coram nobis, coram vobis, coram non judice, coram populo; many states have replaced the writ with a single post-conviction motion
entries.see also: ex parte, sub, ad, in re, before

entries.respell: KUUM (rhyming with room for most Americans); KUM also heard
entries.meaning: Latin "with, combined with." The living English use is the hyphenated compound noun naming one thing that does two jobs, and it is the only genuinely productive Latin preposition left in the language — productive, but not much used.
examples: They converted the garage into a workshop-cum-guest-room.
He served for years as chauffeur-cum-bodyguard.
She runs a bookshop-cum-café on Third Street.
The building is a chapel-cum-concert-hall with terrible acoustics.
The stock traded cum dividend through Thursday and fell on Friday.
Bonds purchased cum coupon settle at the higher price.

senses.head: Combining two roles in one thing
body: They built a workshop-cum-guest-room over the garage.

senses.head: Securities: carrying the benefit that is about to be detached
body: The stock traded cum dividend through Thursday.
examples: They converted the garage into a workshop-cum-guest-room.

entries.русский: лат. «с» — совмещение двух ролей: кухня-столовая, актёр-режиссёр; бирж. с правом
entries.register: formal or jocular in the compound-noun use; technical in finance; now largely avoided in American English
entries.complement: a single bare noun, normally hyphenated to the noun before it — never a determiner of its own (✗ a bedroom cum a study), never a clause, never a gerund.
entries.pattern: [noun]-cum-[noun] · cum [dividend / rights / coupon] (securities)
entries.contrast: The construction fuses two roles in one object: a kitchen-cum-dining-room is a single room that is both at once, whereas and would list two separate rooms. In securities pricing cum is the exact opposite of ex — a share sold cum dividend carries the coming payment, one sold ex dividend does not. The word is a homograph of a vulgar English term, and that, plainly, is why the compound construction has all but vanished from American writing while surviving in British.
entries.variants: cum laude, magna cum laude, summa cum laude (frozen; not the same construction); cum grano salis ("with a grain of salt," now always Englished)
entries.see also: ex, with, sine, qua

entries.meaning: Latin "from, down from, concerning." It never became a free English preposition, but the four phrases it heads are common enough in American law and journalism that a reader meets one of them most weeks.
examples: English is the de facto language of international air traffic control.
After the coup he was the de facto head of state for three years.
The statute imposed de jure segregation, and the Court struck it down.
A de jure government may control no territory at all.
Questions of law are reviewed de novo on appeal.
The tax court heard the matter de novo and disregarded the auditor's findings.
The shortfall was de minimis, and the auditors passed over it.
A de minimis violation will not support a private right of action.
The bishop's deposition was taken de bene esse in case he did not live to testify.
Ownership passed de facto long before the deed was ever recorded.

senses.head: De facto: in fact, whether or not by law
body: English is the de facto language of air traffic control.

senses.head: De jure: by law; as a matter of legal right
body: The statute created de jure segregation.

senses.head: De novo: from the beginning, with no deference to the decision below
body: Questions of law are reviewed de novo.

senses.head: De minimis: too small for the law to take notice of
body: The court called the shortfall de minimis.
examples: English is the de facto language of international air traffic control.
After the coup he was the de facto head of state for three years.
The statute imposed de jure segregation, and the Court struck it down.
A de jure government may control no territory at all.
Questions of law are reviewed de novo on appeal.
The tax court heard the matter de novo and disregarded the auditor's findings.

entries.русский: лат. «от, о» — только в оборотах: de facto, de jure, de novo, de minimis
entries.register: legal, academic, and journalistic; a bound element inside fixed phrases
entries.complement: only the Latin noun fixed to it — de facto, de jure, de novo, de minimis, de bene esse. It cannot govern an English noun phrase (✗ de the record; write from the record), and it never takes a clause or a gerund. The de of French borrowings (coup de grâce, de rigueur, de trop) is a different word doing a different job and is not this entry.
entries.pattern: de facto [leader / segregation / standard] · de jure [segregation / government] · review de novo · a de minimis [amount / violation]
entries.contrast: The pair to hold onto is de facto against de jure — what is actually the case against what the law says — and the whole American desegregation story turns on it, because Brown struck down de jure segregation and left de facto segregation standing. De novo is not "again" in the loose sense but "from the beginning, giving no weight to what came before," which is why de novo review is the least deferential standard an appellate court applies. De minimis is the front of de minimis non curat lex, "the law does not concern itself with trifles." Against ex, the other Latin word for "from": ex is "out of" a source, de is "down from, concerning."
entries.variants: the English prefix de- (deflate, derail) comes through French and is a different element; de rigueur, de trop, coup de grâce are French, not Latin; de facto is now set roman in most American style guides
entries.see also: ad, ex, sub, ultra, from

entries.meaning: A Latin "from" that survives in four separate trades, each of which has hardened it into a term with a precise and non-obvious meaning.
examples: The price quoted is ex works, Rotterdam; the buyer arranges carriage.
Delivery is ex warehouse, and freight is for the account of the purchaser.
The shares go ex dividend on the fifteenth of the month.
It traded ex rights all week and the price gap confused retail buyers.
A Ming bowl, ex the Sackler collection, sold for four million.
The colt is by Tapit, ex a Distorted Humor mare.
The treasurer serves on every subcommittee ex officio.
The dean sits on the tenure committee ex officio and rarely votes.

senses.head: Shipping: goods taken over by the buyer at the named point, with costs from there on the buyer
body: The price quoted is ex works, Rotterdam.

senses.head: Securities: without the benefit that has just been detached
body: The shares go ex dividend on the fifteenth.

senses.head: Provenance and pedigree: out of a named source or dam
body: A Ming bowl, ex the Sackler collection.

senses.head: Frozen legal and academic phrases
body: She sits on the committee ex officio.
examples: The price quoted is ex works, Rotterdam; the buyer arranges carriage.
Delivery is ex warehouse, and freight is for the account of the purchaser.
The shares go ex dividend on the fifteenth of the month.
It traded ex rights all week and the price gap confused retail buyers.

entries.русский: лат. «из» — торг. с места отгрузки (франко); бирж. без права; из источника, от
entries.register: commercial, financial, legal, and technical
entries.complement: it depends on the sense. In the shipping and securities senses, a bare noun with no determiner — ex works, ex dividend, never ✗ ex the works. In the provenance sense the object is an ordinary noun phrase and takes its determiner normally — ex the Sackler collection, ex a Distorted Humor mare. In the frozen phrases (ex officio, ex post facto, ex rel.) the noun is Latin and fixed. Never a clause, never a gerund.
entries.pattern: ex [named delivery point] (shipping) · ex [dividend / rights / coupon] (securities) · ex [source] (provenance and pedigree)
entries.contrast: Latin ex means "out of, from" and gave English exit, export, and the prefix in ex-president. It is the exact opposite of cum in securities pricing. Against plain out of and from, which took over the whole job: ex survives only where a trade has frozen it into a term of art. The noun an ex, meaning a former spouse, is the same word turned into a noun and is not a preposition.
entries.variants: ex- as a productive English prefix (ex-wife, ex-officio, ex-directory); ex works, ex ship, ex quay, ex warehouse are defined Incoterms; ex ante and ex post (before and after the event) are frozen adverbials with no object; ex parte and ex rel. have entries of their own
entries.see also: cum, de, ex parte, from, out of, per

entries.meaning: Latin "in, on, into." It never became a free preposition in English — English already had its own in — but the phrases it is locked inside are among the most-used Latin tags in American courtrooms and laboratories.
examples: The tumor was still in situ and had not breached the wall of the colon.
The compound was screened in vitro long before any animal work began.
Results in vivo were far weaker than the cell-culture data had promised.
The judge read the disputed memos in camera before ruling on privilege.
He was tried and convicted in absentia and learned of the sentence from a newspaper.
Her degree was conferred in absentia; she was already in Chile.
Civil forfeiture is brought in rem, against the car itself rather than its owner.
The court lacked in personam jurisdiction over the Nevada seller.
Defense counsel filed a motion in limine to keep the prior conviction out of evidence.
A boarding school stands in loco parentis while the term is running.

senses.head: In situ, in vitro, in vivo: where a thing sits, or where a procedure happens
body: The compound was screened in vitro first.

senses.head: In camera: in the judge's chambers; out of public view
body: The documents were reviewed in camera.

senses.head: In absentia: with the person not present
body: He was convicted in absentia.

senses.head: In rem and in personam: against a thing; against a person
body: Forfeiture is an action in rem.

senses.head: In limine: at the threshold — of a motion made before trial to keep evidence out
body: Counsel moved in limine to exclude the photographs.

senses.head: In loco parentis: in the place of a parent
body: The school stands in loco parentis on the trip.
examples: The tumor was still in situ and had not breached the wall of the colon.
The compound was screened in vitro long before any animal work began.
Results in vivo were far weaker than the cell-culture data had promised.
The judge read the disputed memos in camera before ruling on privilege.
He was tried and convicted in absentia and learned of the sentence from a newspaper.
Her degree was conferred in absentia; she was already in Chile.
Civil forfeiture is brought in rem, against the car itself rather than its owner.
The court lacked in personam jurisdiction over the Nevada seller.

A boarding school stands in loco parentis while the term is running.

entries.pronunciation note: no weak form in these phrases: a speaker reaching for a Latin tag pronounces it carefully, so in camera is /ɪn ˈkæmərə/ and never /ən/
entries.русский: лат. «в» — только в оборотах: in situ, in camera, in absentia, in rem, in limine
entries.register: legal, scientific, and scholarly; a bound element inside fixed phrases, never a free preposition
entries.complement: only the Latin noun the phrase was borrowed with — in situ, in vitro, in vivo, in camera, in absentia, in rem, in personam, in limine, in loco parentis, in extremis, in toto. It never takes a clause or a gerund (✗ in camera reviewing the file), and it cannot govern an English noun phrase: that work belongs to English in, a different and fully living word with its own entry in the core file.
entries.pattern: examined in situ · grown in vitro · heard in camera · tried in absentia · a motion in limine · proceedings in rem
entries.contrast: English in and Latin in are the same ancient word arriving twice, but only the English one governs a noun phrase you choose for yourself; the Latin one is welded to its noun and quoted whole, exactly as ad, de, pro, and sub are. Learn the tags in pairs, because each is a fork in the road: in vitro (in glass, in a dish) against in vivo (in a living animal); in rem (against a thing, and good against the world) against in personam (against a person, and good only against that person); in situ (still in its original place) against ex situ. And mind the false friend: in camera means "in chambers," out of public view — the reverse of what "on camera" suggests to an American ear.
entries.variants: the English prefix in- is a different element; in re has its own entry in the reference file; American style now sets in vitro, in situ, and in absentia roman rather than italic
entries.see also: ad, de, sub, in re, in

entries.meaning: Latin "below." It points the reader down the page, or forward through the article, to something the writer has not said yet — a promise of proof rather than a citation of it.
examples: See infra note 42 and accompanying text.
The point is developed infra Part III.
That objection is taken up infra, at pages 118–24.
Infra Chapter 6 collects the state statutes.
The footnote reads simply "But see infra note 91."
Journals ask authors to write below in the text and keep infra for the notes.
A brief that cites a case infra has usually mis-cited it; the Bluebook wants a short form instead.
entries.pronunciation note: no weak form: it is read as a quoted Latin tag, with a clear first vowel
entries.русский: книжн., юр. ниже (по тексту) — отсылка вперёд, к ещё не сказанному
entries.register: scholarly and legal citation
entries.type: marginal (a Latin adverb standing before a citation reference)
entries.complement: a reference to a place later in the same document — a note number, a part, a page range, a chapter — standing immediately after it: infra note 40, infra Part III.B. It cannot govern an ordinary noun phrase (✗ infra the statute; write below, where the statute is discussed), and it never takes a clause or a gerund. Used alone after a verb (discussed infra) it is a plain adverb with no object at all, and that is its commonest shape.
entries.pattern: see infra [note / Part / pages] · [proposition], discussed infra · infra Chapter 4
entries.contrast: The pair is supra, earlier in this document, against infra, later in it — and neither ever points outside the document you are holding; for another work you use a short-form citation instead. American legal citation is stricter than it looks: the Bluebook allows supra and infra for books, articles, and legislative history, but not for cases, statutes, or constitutions, which take short forms and id. Scientific and general publishers have replaced both with above and below, and most American editors now prefer the English.
entries.variants: below is the plain equivalent and the one modern American style prefers; vide infra ("see below") in older scholarship; ut infra ("as below") in older legal writing
entries.see also: supra, cf., contra, sub verbo, apud

entries.meaning: Latin "between, among." English took the prefix and left the preposition, which now appears only inside a handful of legal tags — but those tags are common enough that any American who reads a court opinion meets inter alia within a page or two.
examples: The complaint alleges, inter alia, breach of fiduciary duty and unjust enrichment.
The partners' rights inter se are governed by the operating agreement, not by statute.
She created an inter vivos trust rather than leaving the property by will.
The ruling binds the parties inter partes and settles nothing for anyone else.
The statute lists, inter alia, fraud, duress, coercion, and undue influence.
Gifts made inter vivos within three years of death are pulled back into the estate.
Shareholders may restrict transfers inter se without binding anyone outside the agreement.
An inter partes review is adversarial, unlike ex parte reexamination.

senses.head: Inter alia: among other things — by far the commonest, and always parenthetical
body: The complaint alleges, inter alia, breach of fiduciary duty.

senses.head: Inter se: among or between themselves — of the parties' rights against one another rather than against outsiders
body: The partners' rights inter se are governed by the agreement.

senses.head: Inter vivos: between living persons — of a gift or trust taking effect during life rather than at death
body: She created an inter vivos trust.

senses.head: Inter partes: between the parties — binding on them and nobody else
body: The ruling binds the parties inter partes.
examples: The complaint alleges, inter alia, breach of fiduciary duty and unjust enrichment.
The partners' rights inter se are governed by the operating agreement, not by statute.
She created an inter vivos trust rather than leaving the property by will.
The ruling binds the parties inter partes and settles nothing for anyone else.
The statute lists, inter alia, fraud, duress, coercion, and undue influence.
Gifts made inter vivos within three years of death are pulled back into the estate.
Shareholders may restrict transfers inter se without binding anyone outside the agreement.
An inter partes review is adversarial, unlike ex parte reexamination.

entries.русский: лат. «между, среди» — inter alia «среди прочего», inter vivos, inter partes
entries.register: legal and academic; not a free preposition in English
entries.complement: only the Latin noun that the phrase fixes to it — inter alia, inter se, inter vivos, inter partes. It cannot govern an English noun phrase (✗ inter the parties; write between the parties), and it never takes a clause.
entries.pattern: inter alia · inter se · an inter vivos [trust / gift / transfer] · binding inter partes
entries.contrast: The homograph inter meaning "to bury" is a different word with different stress — the verb is in-TUR /ɪnˈtɜr/ (they interred him on Tuesday), the Latin preposition IN-ter. Against intra: inter- crosses between separate things, intra- stays inside one, and the entire reach of federal power in America has turned on the difference between interstate and intrastate commerce. The living English descendants are the prefix inter- and the preposition between.
entries.variants: inter- as a productive English prefix (interstate, international, interlock); inter alia ("among other things") and inter alios ("among other people") are the two genders of one tag, and the neuter inter alia is the one an American reads daily
entries.see also: intra, ex parte, between, amongst

entries.meaning: Latin "within, inside." It never became a free preposition in English at all; it entered as a prefix and stayed one, and the few prepositional survivals are Latin phrases quoted whole.
examples: The board's action was intra vires and cannot be set aside on that ground.
Debate over whether the bylaw was intra vires consumed the whole afternoon.
The transaction was intra-group and was eliminated on consolidation.
Congress may not reach purely intrastate activity on a commerce theory alone.
The drug is administered intravenously over four hours.
He played intramural hockey for three years without ever leaving campus.
The old charter distinguished the citizens intra muros from the households outside the walls.

senses.head: Intra vires: within the powers granted — the corporate and administrative sense
body: The board's action was intra vires.

senses.head: As the bound English prefix intra-: inside one body, state, or system
body: The transaction was intra-group.
examples: The board's action was intra vires and cannot be set aside on that ground.
Debate over whether the bylaw was intra vires consumed the whole afternoon.
The transaction was intra-group and was eliminated on consolidation.
Congress may not reach purely intrastate activity on a commerce theory alone.
The drug is administered intravenously over four hours.
He played intramural hockey for three years without ever leaving campus.
The old charter distinguished the citizens intra muros from the households outside the walls.

entries.русский: лат. «внутри» — intra vires «в пределах полномочий»; как приставка intra- «внутри-»
entries.register: legal and technical; a prefix in English far more often than a preposition
entries.complement: only the fixed Latin nouns vires and muros. It cannot govern an English noun phrase (✗ intra the company; write within the company), and it never takes a clause or a gerund. Everywhere else in English it is the bound prefix intra-.
entries.pattern: intra vires · intra-[noun] as a prefix (intracompany, intrastate, intravenous, intramural)
entries.contrast: The pair to memorize is intra vires, within the powers granted, against ultra vires, beyond them — and ultra vires is far the commoner of the two in American corporate law, because nobody writes an opinion about an action that was perfectly authorized. Against inter: interstate commerce crosses state lines and intrastate commerce does not. The living English equivalent is within.
entries.variants: intra- as a productive English prefix; ultra vires is the opposite term and much commoner
entries.see also: inter, ultra, within, without (= outside)

entries.meaning: Latin for "the things that must be changed having been changed." It transplants a rule into a new setting and licenses in advance the small substitutions the transplant needs — swap the party names, swap the dates, and the borrowed clause reads correctly.
examples: Article 12 applies mutatis mutandis to each Subsidiary.
The procedure for appeals applies, mutatis mutandis, to petitions for rehearing.
The same argument holds mutatis mutandis for the second experiment.
Sections 3 through 7 are incorporated mutatis mutandis into this Schedule.
What was said of the Senate applies mutatis mutandis to the House.
The rules of the Superior Court govern, mutatis mutandis, proceedings before the magistrate.
entries.русский: с необходимыми изменениями — юр., книжн.: правило переносится на новый случай
entries.register: legal and academic
entries.type: marginal (a Latin ablative absolute working as an adverbial)
entries.complement: none. It takes no object at all. It modifies a whole clause — usually one saying that a rule applies somewhere new — and it is never followed by a noun phrase or a clause of its own. Where a target has to be named, the preposition doing that work is to: applies mutatis mutandis to the Subsidiary.
entries.pattern: [clause], mutatis mutandis. · [rule] applies mutatis mutandis to [noun phrase].
entries.contrast: The nearest English is with the necessary changes made, or the workaday as applicable. Keep it clear of ceteris paribus ("other things being equal"), which holds variables still while you argue, and of pari passu ("on an equal footing"), which ranks claims against one another. It is a preposition only by courtesy, and it is in this file because the reader will meet it filed among prepositions elsewhere.
entries.variants: mutatis mutandis is the only form — mutandis mutatis is an error
entries.see also: pro, inter, subject to, in accordance with

entries.meaning: The one Latin preposition that became ordinary English. Four senses, and they sit at very different heights of formality — the first is on every gas pump in the country, the fourth is in the probate code.
examples: Tickets are forty dollars per person, and children under six are free.
The car gets thirty-four miles per gallon on the highway.
Interest accrues at six percent per year until the note is paid.
Per your instructions, I canceled the standing order.
The report was filed per the court's scheduling order.
The samples were prepared per the manufacturer's protocol.
Shipped per certified mail on the third of the month.
Notice may be given per facsimile or per overnight courier.
He was twenty minutes late, per usual.
Federal spending per capita rose for the fourth straight year.
The estate passes per stirpes to the children of the deceased brother.
The witness fee is fifty dollars per diem plus mileage.

senses.head: For each — the distributive sense, and by far the commonest
body: Tickets are forty dollars per person.

senses.head: According to; on the authority or instruction of
body: Per your instructions, I canceled the order.

senses.head: By means of — an older commercial sense, now mostly confined to shipping and correspondence
body: Shipped per certified mail on the third.

senses.head: Inside frozen Latin phrases, where it keeps its original force
body: Federal spending per capita rose again.
examples: Tickets are forty dollars per person, and children under six are free.
The car gets thirty-four miles per gallon on the highway.
Interest accrues at six percent per year until the note is paid.
