entries.русский: за, на, с (каждого) — распределительное: per person «с человека»; согласно, по; посредством
entries.register: neutral in the distributive sense; business or formal in the "according to" sense
entries.complement: in the distributive sense, a bare singular count noun with no article — per person, per mile, per year, never per a person. In the "according to" sense, a full noun phrase with a determiner is normal — per the contract, per your email. Never a finite clause (✗ per we discussed; write per our discussion), never a gerund.
entries.pattern: [amount] per [unit] · Per [noun phrase], [clause]. · [clause] per [noun phrase] · [Latin noun]: per capita, per diem, per se, per stirpes
entries.contrast: The distributive per competes with the indefinite article — sixty miles an hour, twice a week — which is what Americans actually say; per is what the label, the invoice, and the speedometer print. In the "according to" sense it competes with according to and in accordance with and is the shortest of the three, though some readers still hear it as businessese. As per is this same word with a redundant as bolted on. The clipped per usual is an American joke made out of as per usual.
entries.variants: a / an is the everyday spoken equivalent in the distributive sense; p.a. abbreviates per annum on financial documents; the frozen Latin phrases built on it — per se, per capita, per diem, per stirpes, per curiam — take no object of their own, and per procurationem has an entry below
entries.see also: as per, per annum, according to, in accordance with, by

entries.meaning: Fixes a rate to an annual period, in the one register where the difference between an annual rate and a total matters legally. It is a fossil of the same construction that gives per capita and per diem, and like them it takes no object of its own.
examples: The note bears interest at 7.5 percent per annum from the date of default.
Rent escalates three percent per annum over the term of the lease.
The trust distributes forty thousand dollars per annum to each beneficiary.
Judgment shall bear interest at the statutory rate per annum until satisfied.
The endowment spends four percent per annum of a trailing three-year average.
Ground rent of one peppercorn per annum was reserved in the original grant.
entries.русский: в год, годовых — фин./юр. о ставке; дополнения не берёт, объект уже внутри
entries.register: formal, financial, and legal
entries.complement: none — annum is already the object of per, so the phrase is complete. It attaches to a rate or an amount that comes before it and cannot govern anything of its own (✗ per annum the loan).
entries.pattern: [rate or amount] per annum · [amount] per annum, [clause] · interest at [rate] per annum
entries.contrast: Ordinary American English says a year or per year; per annum is what the promissory note says, and it is the wording courts look for when they compute post-judgment interest. Its siblings are per diem (a day — which in American usage is also a noun, the daily travel allowance), per mensem (a month, rare), and per capita (a head). Note carefully that per annum means "each year," not "in the first year": six percent per annum on a five-year note is six percent every one of those years.
entries.variants: p.a. is the standard abbreviation on financial documents; per year and a year are the plain equivalents; per diem, per mensem, per capita are the parallel forms
entries.see also: per, as per, of

entries.respell: almost always said as the letters p.p. /ˌpi ˈpi/
entries.meaning: Latin "by the agency of." An American meets it as the little p.p. typed beside a signature on a letter that its signer did not write, and on old bills of exchange accepted by a clerk.
examples: The letter went out p.p. the managing partner, who was in Geneva that week.
Her assistant signed the acknowledgment per pro the department chair.
Bills of exchange were once accepted per procurationem by a clerk holding written authority.
A signature p.p. binds the principal only so far as the authority actually granted reaches.
Bank forms still ask whether the signer executes in person or per pro.
Plain-language guides say to drop the p.p. and type for before the principal's name.
Anyone taking a bill signed per procurationem was on notice to ask what the agent's authority was.
entries.русский: по доверенности, за (p.p. перед подписью) — письмо подписано другим лицом
entries.register: formal and commercial — signature blocks, correspondence, and older negotiable instruments
entries.complement: the name of the principal on whose authority the signature is given — never a clause, never a gerund. It stands immediately before that name in the signature block, with the agent's own signature above or beside it.
entries.pattern: [agent's signature] · p.p. [name of the principal] · signed per pro [firm name]
entries.contrast: The Latin is "through the agency of," and the strict form is agent signs, p.p. principal: the abbreviation names the person who is bound, not the person holding the pen. Office practice on both sides of the Atlantic inverted it decades ago, so letters now go out as p.p. [the assistant's name], and no one reads the abbreviation strictly any more. Distinguish by and through, the litigation formula that names the lawyer through whom a party appears, and on behalf of, the plain modern English that every American style guide recommends instead. Do not confuse it with per curiam, an opinion issued by the court as a body rather than by a named judge.
entries.variants: p.p., pp., per pro, per proc. are the written forms; for and on behalf of are the plain replacements; attorney-in-fact names the underlying authority a p.p. signature claims
entries.see also: by and through, on behalf of, vice, per, pro

entries.meaning: A Latin "for" that never made it into free English but is preserved intact inside a set of phrases every American lawyer uses daily and every American voter has heard at least once. Six of them carry the whole word.
examples: She took the eviction case pro bono.
The firm asks fifty pro bono hours a year of every associate.
Losses are allocated pro rata among the members according to capital account.
Unused premium is refunded pro rata if the policy is canceled early.
He appeared pro se and was outmatched from the first motion.
Courts read pro se filings liberally, but the deadlines still apply.
The president pro tempore of the Senate signed the enrolled bill.
She chaired the meeting pro tem while the chair was in surgery.
The company issued pro forma financial statements reflecting the merger.
The vote was pro forma; the outcome had been settled a week earlier.
Out-of-state counsel was admitted pro hac vice for this matter only.
His pro hac vice application was denied because of the earlier sanction.

senses.head: Pro bono (publico): for the public good — of legal work done free
body: She took the eviction case pro bono.

senses.head: Pro rata: in proportion; share for share
body: Losses are allocated pro rata.

senses.head: Pro tempore, clipped pro tem: for the time being
body: The president pro tempore signed the bill.

senses.head: Pro forma: as a matter of form; on assumed rather than historical figures
body: The company issued pro forma statements.

senses.head: Pro se: on one's own behalf, without a lawyer
body: He appeared pro se.

senses.head: Pro hac vice: for this occasion only
body: Counsel was admitted pro hac vice.
examples: She took the eviction case pro bono.
The firm asks fifty pro bono hours a year of every associate.
Losses are allocated pro rata among the members according to capital account.
Unused premium is refunded pro rata if the policy is canceled early.
He appeared pro se and was outmatched from the first motion.
Courts read pro se filings liberally, but the deadlines still apply.
The president pro tempore of the Senate signed the enrolled bill.
She chaired the meeting pro tem while the chair was in surgery.
The company issued pro forma financial statements reflecting the merger.
The vote was pro forma; the outcome had been settled a week earlier.
Out-of-state counsel was admitted pro hac vice for this matter only.
His pro hac vice application was denied because of the earlier sanction.

entries.русский: лат. «за, вместо» — pro bono, pro rata, pro tempore, pro forma, pro se, pro hac vice
entries.register: legal and technical inside fixed phrases; the free word is an adverb or a noun, not a preposition
entries.complement: only the Latin noun that the phrase fixes to it — pro bono, pro rata, pro tempore, pro forma, pro se, pro hac vice. It cannot govern an English noun phrase (✗ pro the plaintiff; write for the plaintiff), and it never takes a clause.
entries.pattern: pro bono · pro rata · pro se · pro tem · the pros and cons (nouns, not prepositions)
entries.contrast: Latin pro means "for, on behalf of, in proportion to" and is the pro- of pronoun and proponent; English for took over its entire job, which is why the free preposition never survived. Against contra, its Latin opposite, and note that the everyday pair is pros and cons, both of them nouns. Watch the American shortenings: pro bono publico is always cut to pro bono, pro tempore to pro tem, and pro hac vice is said proh-hahk-VEE-chay or -VY-see depending on where the speaker went to law school.
entries.variants: pro- as an English prefix (pro-rate, pro-forma as adjectives); pro tem is the usual clipping of pro tempore; pro tanto ("to that extent") and nunc pro tunc ("now for then," of an order backdated to correct the record) are frozen adverbials that govern nothing
entries.see also: contra, ad, for, ex parte, sine, vice

entries.meaning: Latin "as far as, with respect to." English took as to and left quoad to the old reports, the Scottish church courts, and the occasional scholar reaching for a fence around a claim.
examples: The concession binds him quoad hoc and no further.
The statute is preempted quoad hoc, though the rest of the scheme survives untouched.
The chapel was erected as a parish quoad sacra in 1843.
The defenses admit the contract and quoad ultra deny the pursuer's averments.
Older reports say a release operates quoad the covenants only.
A finding good quoad omnia would settle far more than this record can support.
American courts write "as to this" and leave quoad hoc to the nineteenth-century reporters.
entries.pronunciation note: KWOH-ad · no weak form: quoted Latin keeps its full vowels
entries.русский: устар., юр. что касается, в отношении — quoad hoc «в этой части, применительно к этому»
entries.register: legal, ecclesiastical, and academic; rare in American writing and archaic where it appears
entries.complement: in modern use only the Latin noun fixed to it — quoad hoc, quoad sacra, quoad omnia, quoad ultra. Older English legal prose let it take an ordinary noun phrase (quoad the plaintiff), a use no longer current; it never takes a clause or a gerund.
entries.pattern: true quoad hoc · a parish quoad sacra (Scots ecclesiastical) · quoad ultra denied (Scots pleading)
entries.contrast: Latin "as to, so far as concerns." The living English is as to or with respect to, and an American brief will say "as to this point." The one phrase worth knowing is quoad hoc, which fences a proposition off to the single point at hand: a rule true quoad hoc is not true generally, and the concession dies the moment the facts change. Scottish practice keeps two more — a parish quoad sacra is erected for church purposes only and not for civil ones, and quoad ultra closes a pleading by denying everything not already admitted. It has nothing to do with the canon-law quoad hunc / quoad hanc, a finding about one particular spouse.
entries.variants: quoad hoc, quoad sacra, quoad omnia, quoad ultra are the surviving phrases; as to and as regards are the modern English
entries.see also: as to, with respect to, sensu, coram, ad

entries.meaning: Latin "in the sense of." It exists because a name means different things in different hands, and a scientist who uses one has to say whose meaning he is borrowing.
examples: Aster sensu lato once held nearly every North American species now placed elsewhere.
Used sensu stricto the family takes in three genera; sensu lato, more than forty.
The specimens key out to Canis lupus sensu Nowak 1995.
She uses "modernism" sensu stricto, meaning the years between 1910 and 1930.
The name is applied here sensu Simpson, not sensu Gregory.
Field guides give the species sensu lato and leave the arguments to the monographs.
A record published sensu an author whose types were later lost is worth very little.

senses.head: With stricto or lato: in the narrow or the broad circumscription of a name
body: Used sensu stricto, the family takes in three genera.

senses.head: With an author's name: in the sense that author gave the term
body: The specimens key out to Canis lupus sensu Nowak 1995.
examples: Aster sensu lato once held nearly every North American species now placed elsewhere.
Used sensu stricto the family takes in three genera; sensu lato, more than forty.

entries.pronunciation note: SEN-soo · no weak form: it is quoted Latin, spoken with care
entries.русский: науч. «в смысле» — sensu stricto / sensu lato «в узком / широком смысле»
entries.register: scientific — taxonomy and systematics above all; also scholarly prose
entries.type: simple (a Latin ablative working as a preposition)
entries.complement: either a fixed Latin adjective (sensu stricto, sensu lato, sensu amplo) or the name of the author whose usage is meant, normally with a year: sensu Simpson 1945. Never a clause, never a gerund, and it cannot govern an ordinary English noun phrase (✗ sensu the definition above; write in the sense given above).
entries.pattern: [taxon] sensu stricto · [taxon] sensu lato · [taxon] sensu [author, year]
entries.contrast: The pair carries the whole meaning: sensu stricto (s.s.) is the narrow circumscription of a name, sensu lato (s.l.) the broad one, so a genus sensu lato swallows what a genus sensu stricto leaves out. Adding an author's name instead says "as that author used the name," which is how a systematist cites a disputed circumscription without endorsing it. Keep it apart from cf., which flags doubt about identifying a specimen rather than disagreement about a definition, and from apud, which reports where a text is preserved rather than what a name was taken to mean.
entries.variants: s.s. and s.l. are the standard abbreviations; sensu auctorum ("in the sense of authors generally"); sensu Smith non Jones pins the usage to one author against another
entries.see also: cf., apud, quoad, sub verbo, per

entries.meaning: Alive in exactly three phrases. Sine die ends a session with no return date fixed, which is what every American hears reported when Congress adjourns. Sine qua non names the condition without which the thing cannot be. Sine prole marks a line that ended childless, in a will or a genealogy.
examples: The legislature adjourned sine die on the thirtieth of May.
Trust is the sine qua non of the attorney-client relationship.
The hearing was continued sine die and never rescheduled.
The baronetcy lapsed when the last holder died sine prole.
Causation is a sine qua non of tort liability, not the whole of it.
The convention rose sine die at four in the morning.
The pedigree records both sons as having died sine prole, and the estate passed to a cousin.

senses.head: Sine die: with no day fixed for reconvening
body: The legislature adjourned sine die.

senses.head: Sine qua non: the indispensable condition — the thing without which not
body: Trust is the sine qua non of the relationship.

senses.head: Sine prole: without issue; childless — in wills and genealogies
body: The last holder died sine prole.
examples: The legislature adjourned sine die on the thirtieth of May.
Trust is the sine qua non of the attorney-client relationship.
The hearing was continued sine die and never rescheduled.
The baronetcy lapsed when the last holder died sine prole.
Causation is a sine qua non of tort liability, not the whole of it.
The convention rose sine die at four in the morning.
The pedigree records both sons as having died sine prole, and the estate passed to a cousin.

entries.русский: лат. «без» — sine die «без назначения даты», sine qua non «непременное условие»
entries.register: legal and academic; no free use in English
entries.complement: only the Latin noun fixed to it — sine die, sine qua non, sine prole. It cannot take an English noun phrase (✗ sine a date; write without a date), and it never takes a clause.
entries.pattern: adjourn sine die · a sine qua non of [noun phrase] · [name] died sine prole
entries.contrast: Latin sine is "without," and its descendant through French is sans; the plain modern word is without. Do not confuse it with the trigonometric sine /saɪn/, which comes from Latin sinus and is a different word, though the sine in sinecure (from sine cura, "without care") is genuinely this one.
entries.variants: sine qua non takes a plural sine quibus non in strict Latin, never used in English
entries.see also: sans, without, cum, pro, sub

entries.meaning: Latin "under." English kept the prefix and kept under, and left the bare preposition to four courtroom and citation tags — one of which, sub rosa, has walked out of the courthouse into ordinary speech.
examples: Counsel declined to comment on a matter sub judice.
The motion is sub judice, and the record remains sealed until it is decided.
The panel overruled its earlier holding sub silentio and never said so.
Two footnotes abandon the doctrine sub silentio.
The district court's ruling was affirmed sub nom. Carrillo v. Bettendorf.
It is reported sub nom. In re Estate of Whitfield.
The negotiations were conducted sub rosa for eleven months.
He kept the arrangement sub rosa even from his own partners.
The bequest was accepted sub modo, subject to the conditions attached to it.

senses.head: Sub judice: before the court and not yet decided
body: Counsel would not discuss a matter sub judice.

senses.head: Sub silentio: silently; without saying so — of a holding abandoned unacknowledged
body: The panel overruled its earlier decision sub silentio.

senses.head: Sub nomine, abbreviated sub nom.: under the name of, in citation
body: Affirmed sub nom. Carrillo v. Bettendorf.

senses.head: Sub rosa: in secret; off the record
body: The negotiations were conducted sub rosa.
examples: Counsel declined to comment on a matter sub judice.
The motion is sub judice, and the record remains sealed until it is decided.
The panel overruled its earlier holding sub silentio and never said so.
Two footnotes abandon the doctrine sub silentio.
The district court's ruling was affirmed sub nom. Carrillo v. Bettendorf.
It is reported sub nom. In re Estate of Whitfield.
The negotiations were conducted sub rosa for eleven months.
He kept the arrangement sub rosa even from his own partners.
The bequest was accepted sub modo, subject to the conditions attached to it.

entries.русский: лат. «под» — sub judice «в производстве суда», sub nomine, sub rosa «тайно»
entries.register: legal and academic; a bound element and, far more often, an English prefix
entries.complement: only the Latin noun fixed to it — sub judice, sub silentio, sub nomine, sub rosa, sub modo. It cannot govern an English noun phrase (✗ sub the statute; write under the statute), and it never takes a clause or a gerund. Everywhere else in English it is the bound prefix sub-.
entries.pattern: a matter sub judice · overruled sub silentio · reported sub nom. [case name] · kept sub rosa
entries.contrast: Latin sub is "under," and English under took the entire job — which is why hereunder and thereunder are built on the English word and not on this one. In American citation sub nom. is the workhorse, marking a case that changed names on the way up — as happens whenever a suit against an official in his official capacity is decided under his successor's name. Sub silentio is a term of criticism: it says a court abandoned a holding without admitting it. Sub rosa has escaped law altogether and now just means "in secret." One transatlantic warning: sub judice in Britain names a real reporting restriction that bars comment on a pending case, while in the United States the First Amendment leaves commentators free, so an American who says a matter is sub judice is declining to comment, not citing a rule.
entries.variants: sub- as a productive English prefix (subcontract, sublease, subsidiary); sub nom. is the standard citation abbreviation for sub nomine and governs the case name; sub verbo / s.v. has an entry of its own; subpoena is sub poena, "under penalty," fused into a single word
entries.see also: ad, de, ultra, under, hereunder

entries.respell: nearly always cited as s.v. /ˌɛs ˈvi/
entries.meaning: Latin "under the word." It is the citation form for anything arranged alphabetically, and the one Latin tag a humanities student uses before learning any of the others.
examples: Oxford English Dictionary, 3rd ed., s.v. "preposition."
Black's Law Dictionary, 11th ed., s.v. "estoppel."
The definition appears in Webster's Second, s.v. "gerund."
See the Encyclopaedia Britannica, s.v. "Pelagianism," for the fuller history.
Chicago style asks for s.v. rather than a page number in an alphabetically arranged work.
The note cites two entries at once: s.vv. "tort," "trespass."
Spelled out in full, the citation reads sub verbo "consideration," which almost nobody writes any more.
entries.русский: библиогр. «под словом» — в словарной статье на такое-то слово; сокр. s.v.
entries.register: scholarly citation — dictionaries, encyclopedias, and other alphabetically arranged reference works
entries.complement: the headword being cited, normally in quotation marks: s.v. "estoppel". Never a clause, never a gerund. Two or more headwords take the plural abbreviation s.vv.
entries.pattern: [reference work], s.v. "[headword]" · sub verbo [headword] · s.vv. "[word]," "[word]"
entries.contrast: The point of it is practical: a dictionary or encyclopedia repaginates with every edition, so you cite the entry rather than the page, and the reader finds it in any printing. The competing Latin is sub voce, "under the word," which means the same thing and shares the abbreviation. Distinguish the other sub tags — sub nom. points at a case name and sub judice at a pending matter (see sub) — and note the division of labor with apud, which points at an author who preserves a text rather than at a word in a reference book.
entries.variants: s.v. is the usual written form and s.vv. the plural; sub voce is the equally correct Latin behind the same abbreviation; under is the plain English replacement
entries.see also: sub, supra, cf., apud, sensu

entries.meaning: Latin "above." It sends the reader back to something already on the page, and in an American law review it is the commonest Latin word in the footnotes by a wide margin.
examples: Ackerman, supra note 14, at 22.
See supra Part II.B for the full argument.
The definition given supra controls throughout this Article.
As noted supra, the agency never published the rule.
Supra note 3 collects the conflicting circuit decisions.
The Bluebook forbids supra for cases, so a short form does the work instead.
Chicago style would rather you wrote "see above" than supra in the text.
entries.pronunciation note: SOO-pruh · no weak form: it is read as a quoted Latin tag
entries.русский: книжн., юр. выше (по тексту) — отсылка назад, к уже сказанному в этом же тексте
entries.register: scholarly and legal citation
entries.type: marginal (a Latin adverb standing before a citation reference)
entries.complement: a reference to a place earlier in the same document — a note number, a part, a page — standing immediately after it, and in the Bluebook short form an author's name immediately before it: Ackerman, supra note 14, at 22. Never an ordinary noun phrase (✗ supra the opinion), never a clause, never a gerund. Standing alone after a verb (as noted supra) it is an adverb with no object at all.
entries.pattern: [author], supra note [n], at [page] · see supra Part II · discussed supra
entries.contrast: Supra points earlier in the document you are reading and infra later in it. American legal citation is strict about what it may point at: books, articles, and legislative history take supra, but cases, statutes, and constitutions take short forms and id. instead. And keep it apart from the objectless tags that share its footnote — ibid. and id. ("in the same place," the source just cited), passim ("scattered throughout," after a page range), et seq. ("and the following," after the first section of a run), and op. cit. None of those governs anything: they are adverbs, not prepositions, which is why none of them has an entry of its own here.
entries.variants: above is the plain equivalent, and Chicago prefers it in humanities prose; vide supra ("see above") in older scholarship; op. cit. and loc. cit. are the older short forms that supra displaced in American style
entries.see also: infra, cf., contra, sub verbo, apud

entries.meaning: Latin "beyond, on the far side of." It reached English as a prefix and as a one-word adjective, and as a preposition it governs exactly one noun — but that one phrase is the standard American name for an act that exceeded the actor's authority.
examples: The board's guarantee was ultra vires and could not be enforced against the company.
The agency's rule was struck down as ultra vires.
Shareholders sued to enjoin the transaction as ultra vires.
Most state statutes have abolished the ultra vires defense in ordinary contract actions.
Whether the ordinance was ultra vires took three days of argument.
An act ultra vires is void, not merely voidable.
The trustees acted ultra vires in pledging the endowment as collateral.
The arbitrator's award was vacated as ultra petita because it granted relief no party had requested.
A tribunal that rewrites the contract for the parties has ruled ultra petita.

senses.head: Ultra vires: beyond the powers granted — the corporate and administrative sense
body: The board's guarantee was ultra vires.

senses.head: Ultra petita: beyond what was asked — of a court or arbitrator granting more relief than any party sought
body: The award was vacated as ultra petita.
examples: The board's guarantee was ultra vires and could not be enforced against the company.
The agency's rule was struck down as ultra vires.

A tribunal that rewrites the contract for the parties has ruled ultra petita.

entries.русский: лат. «сверх, за пределами» — ultra vires «с превышением полномочий»; ultra petita
entries.register: legal; a prefix and a stand-alone adjective in English far more often than a preposition
entries.complement: only the fixed Latin noun vires — and, in older writing, petita. It cannot govern an English noun phrase (✗ ultra its powers; write beyond its powers), and it never takes a clause or a gerund. As an English word ultra is either a prefix (ultraviolet) or an adjective meaning "extreme" (an ultra position), and neither of those is a preposition at all.
entries.pattern: an act ultra vires · the ultra vires [doctrine / defense] · ultra-[adjective] as a prefix
entries.contrast: The pair is ultra vires, beyond the powers granted, against intra vires, within them — see intra — and in American corporate and administrative law ultra vires is far the commoner of the two, because nobody writes an opinion about an act that was perfectly authorized. Against beyond, the living English word: beyond is spatial and open-ended, while ultra vires is a verdict. Note also that the modern corporate statutes have largely abolished the ultra vires defense between a company and an outsider, while it stays fully alive against a government agency.
entries.variants: ultra- as a productive English prefix (ultramarine, ultrasound, ultraviolet); stand-alone ultra meaning "extreme" is English, not Latin; intra vires is the opposite term
entries.see also: intra, sub, de, beyond, without prejudice to

entries.meaning: Latin "turned toward, against," from vertere. It is the most thoroughly naturalized Latin preposition in the language after per, and its three senses run from the courtroom out into ordinary speech.
examples: Brown v. Board of Education was decided in 1954.
The docket lists Hernandez versus the City of Tucson for Thursday.
Michigan vs. Ohio State kicks off at noon.
The heavyweight bout is Ali versus Frazier all over again.
It is a classic case of speed versus accuracy.
We are still weighing renting versus buying.
The chart plots unit cost versus production volume.
Twelve percent this quarter versus eight percent last year.

senses.head: Legal citation: one party against another
body: Brown v. Board of Education was decided in 1954.

senses.head: Contest: one side against another
body: Michigan vs. Ohio State kicks off at noon.

senses.head: Comparison: one option weighed against another
body: It is a classic case of speed versus accuracy.
examples: Brown v. Board of Education was decided in 1954.

entries.русский: против — юр. в названии дела; в спорте; в сравнении с, или (сокр. vs., v.)
entries.register: neutral; formal in legal citation
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund — never a finite clause (✗ versus he stayed home; write versus his staying home). Because it coordinates, the two sides should be the same kind of phrase: speed versus accuracy, driving versus flying.
entries.pattern: [noun phrase] versus [noun phrase] · [gerund] versus [gerund] · [case name] v. [case name] · [team] vs. [team]
entries.contrast: Three written forms, three habitats. Spelled-out versus belongs to running prose; vs. to sports, science, and everyday shorthand; v. to legal citation — and Americans read v. aloud as "versus," so Brown v. Board is spoken "Brown versus Board," where British lawyers say "and" in civil cases. Against against, which needs no second term to compare; against compared with, which is neutral where versus frames the two terms as rivals.
entries.variants: vs. (general, sporting, scientific); v. (legal citation; American style keeps the period); versus spelled out in running prose
entries.see also: against, contra, vice, in contrast to

entries.meaning: Names a successor and the person succeeded, in the one register that still uses it: the Congressional Record, military promotion lists, the Foreign Service register, and the appointments column of an old newspaper.
examples: To be Colonel: Margaret A. Ruiz, vice Colonel J. T. Nash, retired.
Appointed Ambassador to Portugal, vice Mr. Halloran, resigned.
He takes the chair vice Senator Coburn, deceased.
She was named acting director, vice the incumbent, on administrative leave.
The commission seat went to Ellis, vice Barrow, whose term expired in June.
Lieutenant Park assumes command of B Company, vice Captain Doyle, transferred.
entries.русский: лат. вместо, на место (кого-то) — в списках назначений: сменяя такого-то
entries.register: formal and official; rare, and now confined to military, diplomatic, and civil-service appointment notices
entries.complement: a proper name or a title naming the predecessor — never a clause, never a gerund. It is always parenthetical, set off by commas, and it never begins a sentence.
entries.pattern: [appointment], vice [name of the person replaced], [reason for the vacancy].
entries.contrast: Two different words are spelled alike. This one is Latin vice, "in the place of," the same element as in vice president, vice chair, viceroy, vice admiral, and vice versa; the moral vice /vaɪs/ — and the workshop tool, which Americans spell vise — are unrelated. Its living English equivalents are in place of and in lieu of, both meaning "replacing." It does not mean "on behalf of": that is on behalf of.
entries.variants: vice- fused as a prefix in vice president, vice chair, viceroy is pronounced VYSS; vice versa /ˌvaɪs ˈvɜrsə/ is the same word and keeps the older one-syllable pronunciation
entries.see also: in place of, in lieu of, versus, pro, by and through

entries.meaning: Where an American meets it: hymns and the King James Bible, Twain and Hardy rendering rural speech, a sailing manual, and the charging language of a homicide indictment.
examples: He was gone afore daybreak.
The galley lies afore the mast.
She had worked the whole field afore noon.
Get the hay in afore the rain.
Afore the war, this was all orchard.
Nothing grew on that bottom land afore the flood.
The crew berthed afore the bulkhead and the officers aft of it.

senses.head: Earlier than; before — of time, the ordinary archaic and dialect use
body: He was gone afore daybreak.

senses.head: Nautical: forward of; toward the bow — the one place it is still live technical English
body: The galley lies afore the mast.
examples: He was gone afore daybreak.
The galley lies afore the mast.

entries.русский: устар., диал. до, прежде (о времени); мор. впереди, ближе к носу судна
entries.register: archaic; surviving in nautical usage, in Southern and Appalachian speech, and inside frozen legal compounds
entries.complement: noun phrase or a pronoun in the objective case (afore me). As a conjunction — a separate job — it takes a full finite clause (afore he comes), and that use is still heard in rural speech; the preposition itself never takes a clause.
entries.pattern: afore [noun phrase] · afore the mast (nautical) · the afore[said / mentioned] [noun] (fused, no longer a preposition)
entries.contrast: It is simply the old form of before — the same root with the prefix a- instead of be-, and nothing but three hundred years between them. At sea it means "toward the bow" and is the live opposite of abaft, which is the one place it is still ordinary technical English. In law it survives only welded into aforesaid, aforementioned, and aforethought, where it is no longer a preposition at all — and malice aforethought sits in the murder statute of every American state.
entries.variants: 'fore is the casual respelling of the same word ('fore the storm hit); aforesaid, aforementioned, aforethought are the fused legal survivals
entries.see also: before, ere, prior to, 'gainst

entries.meaning: Places something inside a surrounding mass or a surrounding condition. The choice between amid and amidst carries no difference of meaning at all — only of register, which is exactly why the choice is worth making deliberately.
examples: The bill passed amidst fierce objections from both parties.
She kept working amidst the noise of the renovation.
Amidst the wreckage they found the flight recorder intact.
He resigned amidst rumors of a federal inquiry.
A single oak stood amidst the stumps.
Amidst all the celebration, no one noticed her leave.

senses.head: In the middle of a physical mass of stuff
body: Amidst the wreckage they found the flight recorder.

senses.head: In the middle of a surrounding condition, noise, or state of affairs — now the commoner of the two
body: He resigned amidst rumors of a federal inquiry.
examples: The bill passed amidst fierce objections from both parties.

entries.русский: книжн. среди, посреди — вариант amid, чаще о шуме, обстановке, положении дел
entries.register: literary; not archaic, but the marked member of its pair
entries.complement: noun phrase — characteristically a mass noun, a plural, or an abstract noun. Never a finite clause (✗ amidst he was speaking; write while he was speaking), and never a bare gerund clause (✗ amidst being questioned) — though a deverbal noun with a determiner is perfectly normal, since it is a noun and not a verb form: amidst the shouting, amidst the fighting. It is a preposition only: unlike o'er it has no adverbial use and must have an object.
entries.pattern: Amidst [noun phrase], [clause]. · [clause] amidst [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Two contrasts matter here. Against amid: they are one preposition with two spellings, and American English clearly prefers amid, with amidst running several times rarer and reading as deliberately literary; British usage is more evenly split, so amidst in an American paragraph often signals a writer imitating British prose. Against amongst and among: amid takes what you cannot count — amid the wreckage, amid speculation — while among takes countable individuals you are one of, among the guests. The plain spoken equivalent of both is in the middle of.
entries.variants: amid — the ordinary American form, and the one to use; amidst — literary; midst, 'midst, mid — poetic; British writing uses amidst far more freely than American
entries.see also: amongst, midst, in the middle of, between

entries.meaning: Puts something inside a plurality of separate individuals, without singling any of them out. The -st is a late accretion of the same kind that produced whilst and amidst, and it never carried any extra meaning.
examples: There was a traitor amongst them.
The prize was divided amongst the four finalists.
Amongst the papers she found a letter dated 1912.
He was happiest amongst strangers.
Rumors spread amongst the crew within the hour.
Amongst other things, the report faults the maintenance schedule.
The residue of the estate was split amongst the surviving cousins.

senses.head: In the middle of a group of separate individuals; surrounded by them
body: There was a traitor amongst them.

senses.head: Shared out or distributed to the members of a group
body: The prize was divided amongst the four finalists.
examples: There was a traitor amongst them.
The prize was divided amongst the four finalists.
Amongst the papers she found a letter dated 1912.
He was happiest amongst strangers.

entries.русский: книжн., брит. среди, между — вариант among, о группе отдельных лиц
entries.register: literary; in American prose it reads as an affectation
entries.complement: a plural noun phrase, a collective noun, or a mass of individuals — never a singular count noun (✗ amongst the tree), never a clause, never a gerund. Pronoun objects take the objective case: amongst us, never ✗ amongst we. Like among, it is a preposition only — it has no adverbial life and cannot stand without an object, unlike o'er and withal.
entries.pattern: Amongst [plural noun phrase], [clause]. · [clause] amongst [plural noun phrase] · divided amongst [plural noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Against among: identical in meaning, and American English prefers among by something like ten to one — amongst is the dominant form in British writing and is one of the surest tells that an American is imitating it. Against between: the schoolroom rule that between takes two and among takes three or more is only half right, because between is correct for any number when the relation is one-to-one and reciprocal (a treaty between the seven signatories), while among views the group as an undifferentiated mass (divided among the heirs). Against amidst, which takes uncountable stuff rather than countable individuals.
entries.variants: among — the ordinary American form; amongst — literary and British; 'mongst — poetic
entries.see also: amidst, betwixt, between, inter

entries.meaning: Where you meet it: Shakespeare, the King James Bible ("that there be no strife betwixt me and thee"), hymnody, and mock-antique prose. A modern American who writes betwixt is quoting or joking, with the one exception of the fixed phrase.
examples: There was little love betwixt the two brothers.
Let there be no strife betwixt thee and me.
The cabin sat betwixt the river and the ridge.
Nothing ever came betwixt him and his work.
He is betwixt and between — too old for the draft, too young for the pension.
She has been betwixt and between about the move since February.

senses.head: Between — the archaic preposition, in all the senses of between
body: There was little love betwixt the two brothers.

senses.head: In the fixed objectless phrase betwixt and between: neither one thing nor the other; undecided
body: He is betwixt and between.
examples: There was little love betwixt the two brothers.

He is betwixt and between — too old for the draft, too young for the pension.
She has been betwixt and between about the move since February.

entries.русский: устар. между; в застывшем betwixt and between — «ни то ни сё, ни рыба ни мясо»
entries.register: archaic; alive in American English inside one fixed phrase only
entries.complement: two coordinated noun phrases joined by and, or one plural noun phrase — never a clause, never a gerund. In the fixed phrase betwixt and between it takes no object at all and is no longer a preposition.
entries.pattern: betwixt [noun phrase] and [noun phrase] · betwixt [plural noun phrase] · betwixt and between (fixed adverbial, objectless)
entries.contrast: The archaic twin of between, from the same root as two and twin, and nothing separates them but age. The single place it is still ordinary American English is betwixt and between, meaning "neither one thing nor the other, undecided" — and there it has stopped governing anything. Its clipped poetic form is 'twixt.
entries.variants: 'twixt — the clipped poetic form; between — the ordinary modern word; betwixt and between — the one live American survival
entries.see also: 'twixt, between, amongst, inter

entries.meaning: Where you meet it: Milton, whose invocation puts Siloa's brook fast by the oracle of God; the King James Bible; Bunyan; and the county histories of the eighteenth century, which used it the way a modern guidebook uses just off.
examples: The mill stood fast by the ford, and the road ran past its door.
Milton's opening invocation places the brook fast by the oracle of God.
They camped fast by the river and were gone before light.
Fast by the churchyard wall there was a stone with no name on it.
The cottage lay fast by the shore, close enough to hear the surf all night.
Older county histories put the abbey fast by the bridge, where the parking lot is now.
He kept his horse fast by the door in case the night went badly.
entries.pronunciation note: the t drops between the consonants, as in last night · fast-BY
entries.русский: устар. вплотную к, у самого — fast здесь «крепко, вплотную», а не «быстро»
entries.register: archaic and literary — the King James Bible, Milton, ballads, and eighteenth-century topographical prose
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a place, a landmark, or a person — never a finite clause (✗ fast by the river runs), never a gerund (✗ fast by crossing the ford). The two words cannot be separated by a modifier (✗ fast right by the gate), and the object cannot be dropped: unlike o'er this phrase has no adverbial life.
entries.pattern: [clause] fast by [place] · Fast by [place], [clause].
entries.contrast: The trap is the modern sense of fast. This is the fast of hold fast and stuck fast — firm, close, immovable — so fast by the river means "right at the river," never "quickly past it." Its surviving twin is hard by, the same construction with a different intensifier and the only member of the family a modern American ever meets; both were driven out by close by, right beside, and beside. Where a poet wanted the sense in fewer syllables he reached for nigh unto or bare nigh instead.
entries.variants: hard by is the surviving twin and is treated in the place file; fast beside appears in some older texts; close by and right by are the plain modern words
entries.see also: nigh unto, beside, near, afore, forby

entries.meaning: Where you meet it: Burns, Scott, Stevenson, Hogg, and Hardy. That is the whole list. It is here for completeness, not because any American will ever need to write it.
examples: He kept a dozen sheep, forby the cattle.
There were six of us at table, forby the children.
Forby the rent, there was coal to be paid for.
She walked forby the kirkyard without once looking in.
The road runs forby the mill and over the burn.
He is a good enough fiddler, and a joiner forby.

senses.head: Besides; in addition to
body: He kept a dozen sheep, forby the cattle.

senses.head: Past; alongside — the older spatial sense
body: She walked forby the kirkyard without looking in.
examples: He kept a dozen sheep, forby the cattle.
There were six of us at table, forby the children.
Forby the rent, there was coal to be paid for.
She walked forby the kirkyard without once looking in.
The road runs forby the mill and over the burn.
He is a good enough fiddler, and a joiner forby.

entries.русский: диал. (шотл.) кроме, вдобавок к; устар. мимо, вдоль
entries.register: archaic and regional — Scots and northern English; effectively unknown in America
entries.complement: noun phrase — never a clause, never a gerund. In the "moreover" sense it stands alone as an adverb with no object, usually at the end of the clause.
entries.pattern: forby [noun phrase] · [clause], and [noun phrase] forby. (adverbial)
entries.contrast: The two senses split cleanly and were taken over by two different English words: "besides, in addition to" went to besides and in addition to, while the older spatial "past, close by" went to past and by. Having lost both jobs, forby had nothing left to do. And do not let the modern heir be confused with its own near-twin: beside is spatial, "at the side of," while besides is additive, "in addition to" — she sat beside him against nobody besides him showed up.
entries.variants: forbye — the commoner Scots spelling; forbys in some northern texts
entries.see also: besides, in addition to, past, by

entries.meaning: Where you meet it: Shakespeare, Milton, Keats, the metrical psalms, and the hymnbook. Anywhere a line had to scan and against was one syllable too long.
examples: He set his shoulder 'gainst the door.
The rain beat 'gainst the pane the whole night through.
Sworn 'gainst his own kin, he would not speak.
'Gainst such odds no army could have held the field.
She leaned 'gainst the gate and waited for the light.
They marched 'gainst wind and weather to the shore.
entries.русский: поэт. против, о — стяжённое against, апостроф отмечает пропущенный слог
entries.register: poetic and archaic; it exists to save a syllable
entries.complement: noun phrase or a pronoun in the objective case — never a clause, never a gerund. Identical to against in every respect except length, and like against it is a preposition only: it has none of the adverbial use that o'er keeps, so it can never stand without an object.
entries.pattern: 'gainst [noun phrase] — in verse, wherever the meter wants one syllable where against would give two.
entries.contrast: Not a separate word at all: a metrical contraction of against, the first syllable elided and the apostrophe marking the loss. Set it beside its companions in the same trick — 'twixt, o'er, 'neath, and e'er for ever. The dialect spelling agin (I'm agin it) is a different thing: it records a pronunciation of the full word, not a contraction, and belongs to rural American speech rather than to poetry.
entries.variants: gainst without the apostrophe in older printings; agin is the dialectal respelling of full against, not a contraction
entries.see also: against, 'twixt, o'er, neath

entries.meaning: Where you meet it: Chaucer, Spenser's Faerie Queene, and Shakespeare — Olivia in Twelfth Night declares her love "maugre all thy pride." Nineteenth-century antiquarians revived it for a decade or two, and then it stopped for good.
examples: Maugre all his boasting, the man never once left the harbor.
She loved him, maugre her father's rage.
Maugre the storm, the fleet stood out to sea.
He held the pass maugre every assault they made on it.
Maugre his years, the old knight rode first into the field.
I will have my say, maugre the whole council.
entries.русский: устар. несмотря на, вопреки — с оттенком вызова и презрения, «назло»
entries.register: archaic; dead in every register of modern American English
entries.complement: noun phrase — never a clause, never a gerund. It cannot be strengthened by of: ✗ maugre of his pride.
entries.pattern: Maugre [noun phrase], [clause]. · [clause] maugre [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: It means what despite and in spite of mean, and it lost to both. What it had that they lack is contempt: the literal sense is "in the ill will of, in defiance of," so maugre all thy pride is not a neutral concession but a taunt. Compare notwithstanding, the one concessive of this vintage that survived, and survived by moving into law.
entries.variants: mauger, maulgre, malgre in older texts; modern French malgré is the same word
entries.see also: notwithstanding, in spite of, regardless of, without prejudice to

entries.meaning: Where you meet it: hymns, the Book of Common Prayer ("In the midst of life we are in death"), nineteenth-century verse, and the still-current phrase a traitor in our midst, in which it is a noun.
examples: Midst the din no one heard the bell.
He stood 'midst the ruins of his own house.
A stranger appeared 'midst the dancers and was gone again.
There is a traitor in our midst.
In the midst of life we are in death.
She resigned in the midst of the investigation.

senses.head: Poetic preposition: in the middle of; amid
body: Midst the din no one heard the bell.

senses.head: Noun, inside in the midst of and in our midst — where the prepositional work is done by in and of, not by this word
body: There is a traitor in our midst.
examples: Midst the din no one heard the bell.
He stood 'midst the ruins of his own house.
A stranger appeared 'midst the dancers and was gone again.
There is a traitor in our midst.
In the midst of life we are in death.
She resigned in the midst of the investigation.

entries.русский: поэт. посреди, среди; сущ. в оборотах in the midst of, in our midst «среди нас»
entries.register: poetic as a preposition; the noun inside in the midst of is ordinary formal English
entries.type: simple as a preposition; a noun in its ordinary modern use
entries.complement: as a preposition, a noun phrase — never a clause, never a gerund. Note carefully that in the far commoner phrase in the midst of, midst is a noun, and in and of are the prepositions doing the work.
entries.pattern: midst [noun phrase] (poetic) · in the midst of [noun phrase] (the ordinary construction) · in our / their midst
entries.contrast: The bare preposition midst belongs to verse; prose uses in the midst of, a complex preposition built on the noun and parallel to in the middle of. Against amidst and amid, its longer relatives — same root, same sense, different register. The shortest member of the family is bare poetic mid (mid the roses), which no one has written seriously in a century.
entries.variants: 'midst — the commoner poetic spelling; mid — the shortest poetic form; amid and amidst — the prose forms; in the midst of — where midst is a noun
entries.see also: amidst, amongst, in the middle of, neath

entries.meaning: Nothing but a shorter beneath. It has no meaning of its own, only a syllable count, and that is the entire reason it exists.
examples: 'Neath the shadow of the elms we sang the old songs.
He sleeps 'neath the sod of his own field.
The valley lay 'neath a sheet of cloud all morning.
'Neath her window he waited until dawn.
Buried 'neath the church floor, the founder rests there still.
The colors passed 'neath the arch to the sound of drums.
entries.русский: поэт. под — стяжённое beneath, только ради размера стиха
entries.register: poetic and archaic — hymnbooks, nineteenth-century verse, and old college songs
entries.complement: noun phrase — never a clause, never a gerund. It must have an object: unlike o'er, it kept none of the adverbial use of its parent, so ✗ the valley lay 'neath is not English.
entries.pattern: 'neath [noun phrase] — in verse, wherever the meter wants one syllable where beneath would give two.
entries.contrast: A metrical clipping of beneath, exactly as 'gainst is of against and o'er is of over. Modern prose uses under, beneath, or below. The place an American is likeliest to run into it is a hymn ("'Neath the shadow of Thy throne") or an alma mater written in the 1890s, when the college-song idiom was stiff with these forms.
entries.variants: 'neath with the apostrophe is the standard spelling; neath without it appears in later printings; beneath is the full form
entries.see also: o'er, 'gainst, under, midst

entries.meaning: Where you meet it: the King James Bible — Epaphroditus was "sick nigh unto death" — hymnody, nineteenth-century sermons, and the folk register of the rural South and Midwest, where a speaker uses it knowing perfectly well that it is old.
examples: He was sick nigh unto death and did not know anyone for a week.
The old church stood nigh unto the crossroads, with the graveyard behind it.
She has worked that farm nigh unto fifty years.
The creek came up nigh unto the porch steps before it crested.
Getting a straight answer out of him is nigh unto impossible.
Nigh unto midnight the wind dropped and the rain came on.
The old man was nigh unto ninety and still drove himself to church.

senses.head: Close to, in space or in time
body: The old church stood nigh unto the crossroads.

senses.head: Close to a state or condition — above all in the biblical sick nigh unto death
body: He was sick nigh unto death for a week.

senses.head: Almost — before a number or an adjective, in folksy American speech
body: Getting a straight answer out of him is nigh unto impossible.
examples: He was sick nigh unto death and did not know anyone for a week.
The old church stood nigh unto the crossroads, with the graveyard behind it.
She has worked that farm nigh unto fifty years.
The creek came up nigh unto the porch steps before it crested.
Getting a straight answer out of him is nigh unto impossible.
Nigh unto midnight the wind dropped and the rain came on.
The old man was nigh unto ninety and still drove himself to church.

entries.русский: устар. близ, вплотную к — о месте, времени или состоянии: sick nigh unto death
entries.register: archaic and biblical; alive in American speech only as a deliberately folksy intensifier
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a place, a time, a state, or a quantity — nigh unto death, nigh unto midnight, nigh unto fifty years. Never a finite clause (✗ nigh unto he died), and a gerund after it is dialect at best (nigh unto finishing the job belongs to backcountry speech, not to writing). Before an adjective or a bare number (nigh unto impossible, nigh unto sixty) it means "almost," and there it is an intensifier rather than a preposition.
entries.pattern: nigh unto [noun phrase] · sick nigh unto death · nigh unto [number or adjective] (intensifying)
entries.contrast: Nigh is the old positive of near — nigh, near, next were once positive, comparative, and superlative of one word, which is why near still feels like a comparative — and unto is the archaic to that the King James Bible preserved. Put together they mean "close to." Keep the two living descendants apart: nigh in nigh on and nigh onto hedges a stretch of time (nigh on forty years) and is treated in the time file, while nigh unto is the biblical form and reaches for proximity, condition, or degree. Modern prose says near, close to, or almost.
entries.variants: bare nigh (nigh the house); nigh on and nigh on to are the commoner American forms for durations; well-nigh is the fossilized adverb; anigh and anear are the dialect relatives, which belong to the place file
entries.see also: nigh, unto, fast by, afore, near

entries.meaning: Where you meet it: "O'er the ramparts we watched" and "O'er the land of the free" — the national anthem alone keeps this word in the ear of the entire country, which makes it the one archaic preposition every American knows without knowing it. Beyond that, hymns, Poe, Longfellow, and the metrical Psalms.
examples: O'er the ramparts we watched, were so gallantly streaming.
The banner yet waves o'er the land of the free.
He wandered lonely o'er the hills that summer.
A shadow passed o'er her face and was gone.
The bells rang out o'er the sleeping town.
O'er moor and fen, o'er crag and torrent, lead thou me on.
The battle o'er, the field was left to the crows.
The long night at last was o'er.
Word of the surrender spread o'er the whole county before nightfall.

senses.head: Above or across — the spatial senses of over, and the ones the anthem uses
body: O'er the ramparts we watched.

senses.head: Throughout; all over — of sound, light, or anything that spreads across a whole area
body: The bells rang out o'er the sleeping town.

senses.head: Adverb, with no object at all: over, finished — often postposed in verse
body: The battle o'er, they buried their dead.
examples: O'er the ramparts we watched, were so gallantly streaming.
The banner yet waves o'er the land of the free.
He wandered lonely o'er the hills that summer.
A shadow passed o'er her face and was gone.
The bells rang out o'er the sleeping town.
O'er moor and fen, o'er crag and torrent, lead thou me on.
The battle o'er, the field was left to the crows.
The long night at last was o'er.
Word of the surrender spread o'er the whole county before nightfall.

entries.русский: поэт. над, через, по — стяжённое over, только ради размера стиха
entries.register: poetic and archaic — and yet every American hears it several times a year
entries.complement: noun phrase — never a clause, never a gerund. Like over, it can also be an adverb with no object at all (the battle o'er), and in verse that objectless use is often postposed.
entries.pattern: o'er [noun phrase] · [noun phrase] o'er (adverbial, postposed in verse)
entries.contrast: Nothing but a one-syllable over. Where over would give a poet two syllables and the line needs one, o'er appears. Its family is the whole set of poetic elisions — e'er for ever, ne'er for never, heav'n, ev'ry — and the compound o'erhead. It has no separate meaning whatever, and treating it as more solemn than over is a misreading.
entries.variants: oer without the apostrophe in some older printings; o'erhead, o'ercome, o'erthrow in verse compounds
entries.see also: over, neath, 'gainst, 'twixt

entries.meaning: A contraction that lives on the same shelf as o'er and 'neath: it says nothing that upon does not, and it says it in one syllable instead of two. Where it is not verse it is dialect, and in both places the shortening is the whole point.
examples: He laid his hand 'pon the Book and swore.
'Pon my word, I have never heard the like.
A light came 'pon the water and was gone again.
She set the lamp 'pon the sill for him to see from the road.
'Pon my soul, the man has not changed in thirty years.
The ballad has him ride 'pon a milk-white steed.
All that was left 'pon the table was a note and a key.
entries.русский: поэт., диал. на — стяжённое upon; в божбе 'pon my word «честное слово»
entries.register: poetic, archaic, and dialectal — verse, ballads, oaths, and the represented speech of the rural South
entries.complement: a noun phrase or an objective-case pronoun ('pon it, 'pon him) — never a clause, never a gerund. It must have an object: unlike o'er it kept none of its parent's adverbial use, so ✗ the lamp was set 'pon is not English.
entries.pattern: 'pon [noun phrase] · 'pon my word / 'pon my soul (fixed oaths, where the object is frozen in place)
entries.contrast: Nothing but a shorter upon, which is itself an emphatic on — so the ordinary word is two syllables of history away. Its companions are the other metrical clippings, 'gainst, 'neath, 'twixt, and o'er, and like them it exists to save a beat. Where a modern American has actually met it is the mild oath 'pon my word, in stage-Victorian and stage-Southern dialogue, and there it is barely felt as a preposition at all.
entries.variants: 'pon with the apostrophe is the standard spelling; pon without it in later printings; upon is the full form; 'pon my word, 'pon my soul, and Regency 'pon rep are the fixed oaths
entries.see also: upon, on, o'er, 'gainst, neath

entries.meaning: Where you meet it: Shakespeare — Claudius asks the courtiers to stay "sith nor th'exterior nor the inward man resembles that it was" — together with Spenser, Sidney, and the Elizabethan sonneteers. Nothing later than the seventeenth century.
examples: Sith that hour he has not spoken a word to any of us.
Sith the death of the old king, no council has been called.
Much has changed sith our last meeting.
Sith you will not hear me, I will say no more.
Sith it must be so, let it be done quickly.
Sith he is dead, the quarrel dies with him.

senses.head: Temporal: from that time; since
body: Sith that hour he has not spoken.

senses.head: Causal: seeing that; inasmuch as
body: Sith you will not hear me, I will say no more.
examples: Sith that hour he has not spoken a word to any of us.
Sith the death of the old king, no council has been called.
Much has changed sith our last meeting.
Sith you will not hear me, I will say no more.
Sith it must be so, let it be done quickly.
Sith he is dead, the quarrel dies with him.

entries.русский: устар. с тех пор как; поскольку, раз уж (причинное)
entries.register: archaic; extinct since about 1650
entries.complement: as a preposition, a noun phrase naming a time (sith that day). It was far commoner as a conjunction taking a full finite clause (sith you will not hear me), and nearly every surviving example is of that kind. It never takes a gerund.
entries.pattern: sith [noun phrase] (preposition) · sith [clause] (conjunction — the usual case)
entries.contrast: The ancestor of since, which absorbed both of its jobs — the temporal "from that time onward" and the causal "seeing that" — and drove it out by about 1650. It has no connection whatever to the Sith of Star Wars, an invented name, though that is now the only place most Americans have seen the letters in that order.
entries.variants: sithence, sithen, sithens in Middle and early Modern English; since is the modern reflex
entries.see also: since, ere, afore, betwixt

entries.meaning: Where you meet it: Shakespeare and his contemporaries, the metrical psalms, and the occasional Tudor statute. Nowhere later, and never in a modern sentence — the adjective has taken the spelling over completely.
examples: "Thorough bush, thorough brier," says the fairy, meaning through both of them.
They rode thorough the wood and out at the far side of it.
The old statute speaks of goods carried thorough the realm.
Thorough frost and fire the pilgrims went.
A thoroughfare is simply a way thorough — a road that goes all the way out the other end.
Editors who modernize the spelling to through lose the extra syllable the line was built on.
Strafford's policy took its nickname from the word: Thorough, meaning carried all the way.
entries.русский: устар. (шексп.) сквозь, через — старший двойник through; след в слове thoroughfare
entries.register: archaic; dead as a preposition since the seventeenth century, and now a homograph of the ordinary adjective
entries.type: simple (the older two-syllable form of through)
entries.complement: a noun phrase — never a clause, never a gerund. Note what the modern word does instead: thorough today is an adjective (a thorough search) and takes no object at all, which is exactly why the preposition is unusable — a modern reader meets it, takes it for the adjective, and the sentence collapses.
entries.pattern: thorough [noun phrase] (archaic) · thorough-[noun] in the fused survivals (thoroughfare, thoroughbred)
entries.contrast: Through and thorough are one Old English word, þurh, that split on the number of syllables: the short form kept the prepositional job, and the long form drifted into the adjective meaning "carried all the way through," hence "complete." Shakespeare still has the preposition — the fairy in A Midsummer Night's Dream goes "Thorough bush, thorough brier" — and it dies out with his generation. What is left is the fossil inside thoroughfare, a way that goes all the way through, along with thoroughbred and thoroughgoing, and the political nickname Thorough for Strafford's policy under Charles I.
entries.variants: through is the modern preposition; thro' and thru are respellings of through, not of this word; thoroughfare, thoroughbred, thoroughgoing are the fused survivals
entries.see also: through, o'er, neath, afore, 'twixt

entries.meaning: Where you meet it: two proverbs — 'twixt the devil and the deep blue sea and there's many a slip 'twixt cup and lip — plus Shakespeare, Milton, and the hymnbook. It has no meaning of its own beyond between and a shorter line.
examples: He was caught 'twixt the devil and the deep blue sea.
There is many a slip 'twixt cup and lip.
There is little enough to choose 'twixt the two roads.
He stood 'twixt his father and the door.
Peace was made 'twixt the clans that winter.
'Twixt dusk and dark the whole valley went silent.
entries.русский: поэт. между — стяжённое betwixt, только ради размера стиха
entries.register: poetic and archaic
entries.complement: two coordinated noun phrases joined by and, or one plural noun phrase — never a clause, never a gerund.
entries.pattern: 'twixt [noun phrase] and [noun phrase] · 'twixt [plural noun phrase]
entries.contrast: A metrical clipping of betwixt, which is itself the archaic twin of between — three steps, then, from the ordinary word. Its companions in verse are 'gainst, 'neath, and o'er. Modern prose uses between, and the two proverbs below are the only strings most Americans have ever heard it in.
entries.variants: twixt without the apostrophe in later printings; betwixt is the full form; between is the modern word
entries.see also: betwixt, between, 'gainst, o'er

entries.meaning: A survival of the Old English habit of letting a preposition follow its object. Its three uses shade into one another, and only the first is genuinely prepositional.
examples: He had no weapon to defend himself withal.
She gave him money to buy bread withal.
The tools he worked withal were his father's before him.
The room was small, and cold withal.
He is a hard man, and honest withal.
She spoke plainly, and withal kindly.
It was a long book, and a dull one withal.
The terms were harsh, and withal the only ones on offer.

senses.head: Postpositive preposition: with, its object already stated earlier in the clause
body: He had no weapon to defend himself withal.

senses.head: Adverb: besides, moreover, in addition
body: The room was small, and cold withal.

senses.head: Adverb: nevertheless, for all that
body: He is a hard man, and honest withal.
examples: He had no weapon to defend himself withal.
She gave him money to buy bread withal.
The tools he worked withal were his father's before him.
The room was small, and cold withal.
He is a hard man, and honest withal.
She spoke plainly, and withal kindly.
It was a long book, and a dull one withal.
The terms were harsh, and withal the only ones on offer.

entries.русский: устар. с (постпозитивный предлог, объект назван раньше); к тому же; тем не менее
entries.register: archaic and literary
entries.type: postpositive as a preposition; adverb in its commoner use
entries.complement: its object comes first and is separated from it. Withal is a stranded with whose object has already appeared earlier in the clause: the tools he worked withal means "the tools he worked with." It can never be followed by a noun phrase (✗ withal a knife) and never takes a clause. In the adverbial use it has no object at all.
entries.pattern: [noun phrase] ... withal (postpositive preposition) · [clause], [adjective] withal (adverb) · withal, [clause] (adverb, sentence-initial)
entries.contrast: The single most misread word in this file. Modern writers use it as though it were "with all," a vague intensifier meaning something like "altogether" — it is not. It is either a postposed with, its object already gone by, or an adverb meaning "besides, moreover" or "nevertheless." Compare therewith, wherewith, and herewith, which are the same preposition fused to a pointing word instead of stranded, and note the parallel with modern stranding: the tools he worked with is the living construction that replaced it.
entries.variants: wherewithal is the same element, now a noun meaning "the means"; therewith, herewith, wherewith are the fused relatives
entries.see also: with, hereunder, thereunder, notwithstanding

entries.meaning: Where you meet it: the King James Bible ("they led him without the camp"), the hymn "There is a green hill far away, without a city wall," Shakespeare's stage directions, and the statutory phrase within and without the State. Never assume a modern American reader will take it correctly — most will read it as "lacking" and be confused for a line or two.
examples: There is a green hill far away, without a city wall.
They led him forth without the gate and stoned him there.
The suburbs lay without the old walls.
He waited without the door for the better part of an hour.
Business conducted within and without the state is taxed at the same rate.
All the ground without the fortifications had been cleared for a mile.

entries.русский: устар. вне, снаружи, за пределами — утраченный смысл, противоположность within
entries.register: archaic and literary; alive in one legal collocation
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a place or a boundary — never a clause, never a gerund. It also occurs as an adverb with no object at all, chiefly as a stage direction (a noise without). This is a different sense from the everyday privative without, which has its own entry.
entries.pattern: without [place or boundary] · within and without [noun phrase] (the surviving legal pair) · [noise / knocking] without (adverbial stage direction)
entries.contrast: Everything turns on this: the living without means "lacking" (without money), while this archaic one means "on the outside of" (without the walls) and is the exact opposite of within. English lost the spatial sense around 1800 and now says outside of — but the old sense is why within and without still pair off in statutes and insurance policies, and why the outside world was once the world without. The Scots preposition outwith keeps the spatial sense alive north of the border, and it is not a variant an American can borrow.
entries.variants: the spelling is identical to the privative without — only context separates them; outwith is the living Scots equivalent, not standard American
